Mynt admins can send a firm back to `sandbox`, never to live, and the firm is told (`partner_ledger.source_changed`).

Every change is audited. The kit's tools and `register_partner_signing_key` need the firm to be active.

### Who can change what Mynt reads as a firm's books

A licence provider's own member, and only after a **member cool-off**: `PARTNER_MEMBER_COOLOFF_HOURS` (default 72) from the later of the account's creation and its joining that firm.

Inside the cool-off a member can't:

- register or replace the live key;
- confirm endpoints;
- upload a live daily file;
- switch the ledger source to live.

Test keys, test files and conformance runs are fine: a test key can never sign live books.

### Standing goes with the role

What counts at a licence provider is an account's licence-provider *standing* there (`users.lp_since`), not its roles or its membership alone.

- A firm's first ever licence provider has standing at once, and that marks the firm established. `entities.lp_established_at` is set in the same transaction with the firm's row locked, and was backfilled for firms that already had a licence provider.
- After that, standing comes only through a request (`firm_member_requests`) that an existing licence provider accepts with `decide_firm_member`. Declining ends the request and removes the account from the firm.
- This holds even if every licence provider the firm had has since lost the role.
- It holds whichever way the account got there: added by a Mynt admin as a licence provider, or already a member (say as a consumer) whose roles later gain `license_provider` through an invite applied at its next sign-in.

Until it is accepted, the account has no licence-provider powers at all. Mynt resolves its roles without `license_provider` (`rolesWithStanding` in `core/src/store.ts`, applied to every account read from the store and to each session's tools). So the account:

- gets none of a licence provider's tools;
- can't open sealed product-health or pool figures;
- can't approve or decline sponsorships, set covenants, revoke under a breach, register a key or decide anything.

The services that re-read the account refuse it too.

More rules on standing:

- Losing the role ends the standing.
- The one deciding a request must have had standing since before the request was made and be past the cool-off.
- An account that has meanwhile joined another firm can't be accepted.
- The cool-off and the "joined before" order count from the latest of creation, joining and gaining standing.
- Licence providers from before standing existed were given it once, from when they joined.
- Losing standing (the role taken away, or leaving the firm) is recorded (`firm_standing_history`) and told to the firm (`firm.member_standing_lost`).

### When nobody can decide

If no licence provider of the firm has had standing since before a request and is past the cool-off (all of them were demoted, say), the request stays pending. Only a Mynt admin's recovery settles it.

1. The admin calls `recover_firm_member { request_id, reason }`. This tells every current and past licence provider of the firm (`firm.recovery_pending`, as a notice each and on the firm's webhooks) and starts a 7-day wait.
2. During the wait, any past licence provider of the firm, even one whose role has since been taken away, can block it with `block_firm_recovery` (which any signed-in account has). Blocking declines the request. The block is audited and told to the same people.
3. Calling `recover_firm_member` again after the wait completes the recovery.

A recovery, started or completed, is refused:

- while the firm has someone who can decide;
- while any past licence provider of the firm (other than the account the request is for) can't sign in: its whitelist entry is gone or its sign-up is blocked, as `revoke_user` does;
- for 30 days after any of them lost standing there through a Mynt admin's action.

An admin's action here means: moved to another firm by `add_entity_member` (whose result says so), roles rewritten by an invite (including being made an admin, `admin_promoted`), or revoked (`revoke_user` ends standing too).

Further rules:

- Completion re-checks the lock and the deciders, and makes the grant, in one transaction with the firm's row locked.
- A past licence provider can block even if it holds the admin role now, but not a recovery it started.
- The cause is kept in `firm_standing_history`. The refusal names the reason, never the person.
- A recovery takes one Mynt admin, not two. A second admin's sign-off would be stronger and is not built.

### What the firm is told

Each of those steps, every member added or asked for (`add_entity_member`) and every member a Mynt admin takes out is told to the whole firm: an event on its webhooks and a notice to each existing member (`list_firm_notices`).

`remove_entity_member({ entity_id, email })` takes a member out. They stop acting for the firm, a licence provider's standing there ends as `firm.member_standing_lost`, and their sign-in and roles stay. It is audited as `remove_entity_member`, in the workspace class.

The events:

- `firm.member_pending`, `firm.member_added`, `firm.member_removed`, `firm.member_standing_lost`, `firm.recovery_pending`
- `partner_ledger.endpoint_change_pending`, `partner_ledger.key_changed`, `partner_ledger.endpoints_confirmed`, `partner_ledger.source_changed`, `partner_ledger.approval_requested`, `partner_ledger.conformance_expiring`

### A second approval for live changes

A live key change or a switch to live waits for the approval (`approve_partner_kit_change`) of a licence-provider member who:

- is past the cool-off, and
- became a member before the requester did, by effective join time (the later of creation and joining).

So two accounts that joined together can't approve each other.

How requests behave:

- A request lasts 7 days. A newer request of the same kind, or a direct registration, supersedes older ones.
- Approving a live key change claims the request, changes the key and marks it approved in one transaction.
- Approving a switch claims it (`approving`, with `approving_at`), makes the switch with every check again, and puts it back to `pending` if that fails. A decline can't land under a change in flight.
- A request left `approving` for more than 10 minutes is put right from what is actually there: approved if the key or source it asked for is in place, otherwise back to `pending`.

The firm's earliest member, and a one-member firm's only member, need no approval. That is safe only because nobody joins a firm with members without one of them accepting it.

A key ever registered as a test key, by any firm, is never accepted as a live key, and the other way round. Each history is kept, MACed.

### What is left: the insider

These controls stop an account added to a firm, by a Mynt admin or anyone else, from quietly taking over its books. It waits out the cool-off in plain view of the firm's existing members and, where there are two, needs the other's approval.

They don't stop:

- a firm's earliest member, or a one-member firm's only member, past the cool-off;
- two long-standing members acting together;
- a Mynt admin who bootstraps a firm's first ever licence provider (an empty firm has nobody to ask);
- a Mynt admin's recovery that nobody who has been a licence provider at the firm blocks in its 7 days.

Such a person can register a key and serve figures the firm's real books don't support. Those figures read verified, which drives pools' reserve checks.

Mynt can't tell a firm's own people from its books. A firm that wants more should keep at least two members and act on its notices.

### Covenants on a sandbox ledger

A published product is never judged on sandbox figures. A sandbox-sourced snapshot reads `unknown` ("the sponsor's ledger isn't live"), not sandbox. Past a pause rule's unknown limit it pauses the product, because only the licence provider can end it, by connecting its books. Every other unknown still only alerts.

An unpublished product is judged sandbox-only by the snapshot's own `source`, and without a snapshot by the ledger the firm is on now. A ledger Mynt can't tell is never taken for sandbox.

### Running out

A firm on a live source is:

- warned once, `PARTNER_CONFORMANCE_WARN_DAYS` (default 7) before its pass runs out (`partner_ledger.conformance_expiring`);
- told once when it has run out and its snapshots went back to the sandbox (`partner_ledger.source_changed` with `reason: conformance_expired`).

## Money rails

This file covers the pre-approved rails money moves on, the one check every money movement passes (the chokepoint), what a licence provider must supply before a live movement, and the money ledger. It is for licence providers, builders and Mynt admins.

See also: [Firms, licences and licence providers](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/licence-providers.md), [Liquidity pools and on-chain treasuries](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/liquidity-and-treasury.md), [Vendors and the marketplace](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/vendors-and-marketplace.md), [Runtime API](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/runtime-api.md).

Money moves off-chain only, through rails a Mynt admin has approved. Solana programs never move money, and Mynt never holds customer funds: it instructs the licence provider's rail. Rails, the chokepoint and the ledger are in `core/src/money-rails.ts`.

### Rails

A rail is a pre-approved way money moves. It belongs to a licence provider's firm.

#### What a rail holds

| Field | Values |
| --- | --- |
| `kind` | `ramp_adapter`, `ach`, `wire`, `rtp`, `fednow`, `push_to_card` |
| `provider` | For a `ramp_adapter` rail, a ramp adapter id (`bridge`), or, for a ramp partner speaking Mynt's wire contract itself, the id of its transfer offering |
| `direction` | `on_ramp`, `off_ramp`, `payout`, `deposit` |
| States | The US states it may be used in, as ISO 3166-2 codes such as `us-ny` |
| Limits | A per-transfer limit and a daily limit, in integer US cents. The day is the UTC day |
| `status` | `proposed`, `approved`, `suspended`, `revoked` |
| Approval | Who approved it and when |

#### Which rails Mynt instructs

Mynt instructs transfers only on `ramp_adapter` rails: through a ramp adapter, or through a ramp partner speaking the wire contract. See [The Mynt Ramp](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/vendors-and-marketplace.md#the-mynt-ramp).

Mynt instructs no `ach`, `wire`, `rtp`, `fednow` or `push_to_card` rail. Those can be proposed and approved. A liquidity pool's movements on them are authorised and recorded by Mynt, moved by the sponsoring licence provider on its own rail, and settled by its `report_pool_movement`. See [Liquidity pools](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/liquidity-and-treasury.md#liquidity-pools).

#### Licence coverage of a rail

Each of a rail's states must be covered by a licence of the firm that:

- is verified and in force;
- grants `us_money_transmission` in the regulatory model;
- has its prerequisites held (the FinCEN registration);
- reaches the state: its type names that state, or it is a federal charter whose type covers `us`.

Further rules:

- A licence that reaches a state or the country without that grant counts for nothing.
- A federal regulator's licence type that doesn't set `covers` isn't counted anywhere. `approve_rail` says so, and the fix is to set it in the regulatory model.
- Valid states are the 50 states and DC. The territories aren't, until the model has licence types for them.
- Montana is valid, but has no state money transmitter licence, so a rail there can't be approved at present.

#### Rail tools

| Tool | Who | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `propose_rail` | Licence provider | Proposes a rail for its firm. One live rail per firm, kind, provider and direction; to change one, revoke it and propose again. The result lists any `outside_licence_coverage` |
| `list_rails` | Licence provider, Mynt admin | Its own firm's rails; a Mynt admin sees all |
| `approve_rail` | Mynt admin | Approves a proposed rail, or puts a suspended one back. Refused, naming the states, if the firm holds no licence to transmit money in any of them. Whoever proposed the rail, or belongs to its firm, can't approve it |
| `suspend_rail`, `revoke_rail` | Mynt admin | Stop new movements at once. Movements in flight aren't cancelled: the result lists them as `in_flight` |
| `list_money_movements` | Mynt admin, licence provider, builder | The ledger, scoped: a Mynt admin all, a licence provider what it sponsors, a builder its firm's products |

Every rail change, and every refused approval, is in the audit log.

### The chokepoint

Every money movement goes through `authorizeMovement`. That means every service type a Mynt admin declared `moves_money: true` (`onramp_transfer`, `offramp_transfer`), whether its ramp partner runs through an adapter or the wire contract.

`define_service_type` makes every non-quote `ramp` type declare `moves_money`, and any type whose key or name says it moves money. A quote can't declare it or be named as a transfer. See [Declaring what moves money](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/vendors-and-marketplace.md#declaring-what-moves-money).

#### The four conditions for a live movement

In live, a movement is refused unless all of these hold:

1. **A verified home state.** A licensed partner has verified the customer's home state in an identity check (see [Partner requirements](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/money-rails.md#partner-requirements)).
2. **A sponsorship covering that state.** A licence provider has an approved sponsorship covering that state, of the component the action serves. An action that names no component is refused: each of a product's `moves_money` actions needs a `handoff_serves_component` connection in its definition.
3. **An approved rail.** An approved rail of that licence provider fits the direction, the kind, the provider and the state, and a licence named on that sponsorship still lets the firm transmit money in the state today.
4. **Within limits.** The amount is within the rail's per-transfer limit and what is left of its daily limit.

#### How the customer's state is decided

`resolveCustomerState` is the one place that decides the customer's state, afresh for every attempt.

- For live, only the verified state counts. It is recorded on the movement with `state_source: partner_verified`, the verifying partner and when.
- What a customer types (`residence_state`, through `POST /v1/client/fields`) is for sandbox mode and pre-filling forms only. It is marked `self_reported` and never satisfies a live check.
- A movement already in flight keeps the state it was reserved under.
- Erasing a customer's data takes their verified state and their ramp link with it.

The one exception is a liquidity pool's own deposit or withdrawal, which is a firm's money and not a customer's. It goes by the state the firm named, or the state a sponsoring licence provider or a Mynt admin corrected: `liquidity_provider_stated`, `sponsor_corrected`, `admin_corrected`. Those sources are accepted only with a `pool_*` action and a firm's `lp:` reference, so a customer's movement can't claim them.

Every change of state is appended to `customer_state_history` (who, when, old, new):

- It can't be updated, deleted or truncated.
- It never holds up the change it records. An old value that can't be decrypted is marked `old_state_unreadable`.
- Each movement keeps the state it used and where it came from.

#### Refusals

| Refusal (`error` in the API's answer) | Status | Means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `state_unverified` | 403 | Live only: no partner has verified this customer's home state. Nothing else stands in for it |
| `customer_state_required` | 409 | Sandbox mode only (recorded as `would_refuse`): no `residence_state` on file, or not a US state |
| `no_sponsor`, `state_not_sponsored` | 403 | No licence provider sponsors the product, or not in that state |
| `component_required`, `component_not_sponsored` | 403 | The action names no component, or no licence provider sponsors what it serves |
| `no_approved_rail`, `state_not_on_rail` | 403 | No approved rail fits, or none for that state |
| `rail_suspended`, `rail_revoked` | 403 | The rail stopped taking new transfers |
| `licence_not_in_force` | 403 | The sponsorship's licences don't let the firm transmit money in the state today |
| `over_transfer_limit`, `over_daily_limit` | 403 | Over a limit |
| `amount_unknown`, `movement_unknown` | 403 | Mynt can't tell how much it moves, or which way |
| `idempotency_conflict` | 409 | The key was used for a different movement |
| `too_many_attempts` | 409 | This movement has been tried as often as it may be |

The daily limit is checked atomically: a Postgres function locks the rail and adds up the day's ledger inside one transaction.

Each refusal is audited (`money_movement_refused`) and its quote stays usable.

#### Sandbox movements

Movements in sandbox mode never move real money. They go through the same check but aren't refused and use no limit. They are in the ledger with `sandbox: true` and `would_refuse` naming what live would have said.

### Partner requirements

A live movement needs a home state verified by an identity provider its sponsoring licence provider accepts.

#### Which identity providers count

An accepted identity provider is:

- the sponsoring licence provider itself; or
- an offering the licence provider (or a Mynt admin) approved for that sponsorship with `approve_identity_provider`. `revoke_identity_provider` and `list_identity_providers` go with it.

Rules on approval:

- A builder's own firm, or the firm of the person who owns the product, can never be approved for it.
- Nobody approves a provider from their own firm.
- Approval only looks forward. Checks made before it don't count.
- For a ramp, approving any of its firm's adapter offerings approves the firm's one verification record.

Each provider's result is kept separately. The latest from a provider the licence provider accepts is the one that counts, checked per movement. So another provider can't overwrite it, and a check for one licence provider doesn't satisfy another.

#### When a verified state is refused

The movement is refused with `state_unverified` and the reason when:

- that provider's latest check didn't pass (`not_verified`, `no_match` or `deceased`);
- the customer's vault no longer matches what was checked. A keyed hash of the identity details is kept with the verification, so rotating `MYNT_VAULT_KEY` means verifying again;
- the check is older than `VERIFIED_STATE_MAX_AGE_DAYS` (default 365).

A `verified_at` in the future is refused. A check that began before a customer erased their data can't write a state back.

#### Where a verified state comes from

Mynt takes the state from whichever of these says so:

| Source | Supplies a verified state? | What is needed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| An identity service (category `identity` or `kyc`, for example the US `identity_verification` type), with the customer's consent | Yes, if the vendor returns it | The vendor returns `residential_state` (ISO 3166-2, for example `us-ny`) in its output, only when its check verified the address and passed (the device status `verified`). A plain name, date of birth and SSN check doesn't verify an address, so it shouldn't send one. Running the check again is how a state is re-verified |
| A ramp adapter's partner record (`customerIdentity`), read when the customer is linked and before each live transfer | Only if the adapter's partner exposes it | The adapter returns `residential_state` from the partner's verified record. If it can't be read at that moment, what is on file stands |
| Bridge | **No** | See below |
| A ramp partner speaking Mynt's wire contract | Not through the ramp | It offers an identity service as in the first row |
| What the customer typed (`residence_state`) | Never, for live | |

**Bridge.** Bridge's documented `GET /v0/customers/{id}` response has no address. The address is on the create request only, and the response names `address_of_residence` just as a completed requirement. Until Bridge confirms a field carrying the verified residential state (a documented response field, or a report or webhook with it) and it is added to the adapter, customers on Bridge need a separate identity service that returns `residential_state`. Otherwise live movements are refused with `state_unverified`.

### The money ledger

The ledger (`money_movements`) has a row for every movement.

#### What a row holds

- product, sponsoring licence provider, rail and direction;
- `amount_cents` and state;
- a pseudonymous customer key;
- `status`, `external_ref` and timestamps;
- an idempotency key: one quote is one movement.

The customer key is never the builder's reference or a name. It is an HMAC under a key derived from `MYNT_VAULT_KEY`. Rotating that key splits each customer's ledger and state-history rows into before and after, and nothing links the two.

#### Statuses

Statuses only move forward: `requested` → `submitted` → `settled` → `reversed`, or `failed`.

- `failed` frees the amount for the day. Everything else keeps it.
- A retry of a failed movement is the same row.

#### When a movement fails

Only an explicit list of partner refusals marks a movement `failed`: a customer not onboarded, an unknown quote, a refused credential and the like, never behind a 5xx.

Anything else, including a code Mynt doesn't know, leaves it `requested` with `status_detail: outcome_unknown:…`. It is still counted, because the money may have moved. From then on only the partner's own final answer to the current attempt can fail it. A retry being refused, or an earlier attempt failing, says nothing about the attempt in hand.

#### Attempts

- Every attempt's request id is kept, so a settlement or reversal reported against any of them lands.
- One movement can be tried at most 10 times (`MAX_MOVEMENT_ATTEMPTS`). After that, the refusal is `too_many_attempts`.

#### Settlements

- Partners' terminal answers are recorded whatever state the run is in.
- A settlement arriving after Mynt gave up moves `failed` on to `settled`, flagged `late_settlement`.
- A partner's reported total is kept in `settled_amount_cents`. `settled_amount_differs` flags a difference from what was quoted, and is null when the partner doesn't say.

#### Movements nobody answers for

- Movements nobody answers for (48 hours `requested`, 45 days `submitted`) are swept to `failed` with `status_detail: stale_no_answer`.
- A transfer the poller stops waiting for without a void from the partner is `failed` with `status_detail: mynt_gave_up`.

#### Reading the ledger

`flowsFor(productId, from, to)` returns, for live movements requested in `[from, to)`, `flows[direction][status] = { count, amount_cents }`.

A figure that can't be measured is `null`, never 0, with the reason in `not_measured`:

- a period starting before the ledger did;
- an unknown product;
- a direction Mynt doesn't instruct for that product. Money in a builder's own hosted flow is invisible to Mynt.

Swept movements and ones Mynt gave up on are in `unresolved[direction]`, in none of the status totals, because Mynt doesn't know what happened to them.

[Product health](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/licence-providers.md#product-health) reads its flows from here.

pages.title: Agreements
pages.markdown:
This file covers the business agreements between an app and the firms behind its products: their kinds and scopes, the program agreements an app needs before production, e-signature, the oversight audits a licence provider runs under an agreement, and service levels. It is for builders, licence providers and vendors.

See also: [Firms, licences and licence providers](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/licence-providers.md), [Vendors and the marketplace](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/vendors-and-marketplace.md), [Workspaces and sign-in](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/workspaces-and-sign-in.md), [Risk](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/risk.md), [Mynt Studio](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/studio.md).

## App agreements

An app is the distribution layer and **holds no licences of its own**. The financial products it uses are the regulated things, each covered by its own firm's licences or a licence provider's sponsorship. An app's licence coverage is its products'.

What the app's workspace does hold is business agreements with the firms behind those products. Every agreement is for **one app**, whatever its kind, and needs a yes from both sides, like the connector's introductions.

Builders, licence providers and vendors all hold agreement tools. The app's side is the workspace's owners and admins. The other side, the counterparty, is a member of the other firm acting as its licence provider (with standing) or vendor.

### Kinds

| Kind | With | Mynt checks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `program` | A licence provider sponsoring products the app uses | The firm sponsors (an approved sponsorship) every product the agreement names, and the agreement names at least one |
| `vendor` | A vendor firm whose services the app relies on | The firm lists vendor offerings on Mynt. Usually made by accepting the vendor's standard terms when subscribing, already signed by both (see [The marketplace and standard terms](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/vendors-and-marketplace.md#the-marketplace-and-standard-terms)) |
| `data_sharing` | Either of those | The firm sponsors one of the app's products or lists vendor offerings |
| `msa` | Either of those: a master services agreement (MSA) | As for `data_sharing` |
| `sla` | Either of those: a service-level agreement (SLA) | As for `msa`. Its commitments are set with `add_agreement_sla` (see [Service levels](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/agreements.md#service-levels)) |

### Statuses

An agreement is `proposed`, `accepted`, `signed`, `declined` or `terminated`.

An open agreement is one that is `proposed`, `accepted` or `signed`. There is one open negotiated agreement of a kind per app and counterparty. Click-through vendor agreements are one per app and subscription.

### Two sides

Agreements are two-sided: either side proposes, and the side that didn't propose answers. `proposed_by_side` (`app` or `counterparty`) says which proposed.

| Step | Tool | Who |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Propose, from the app's side | `propose_app_agreement` | The app's workspace owners and admins |
| Propose, from a firm | `propose_workspace_agreement` | A licence provider |
| Change the scopes of a proposal | `update_agreement_scopes` | The side that proposed it |
| Respond | `respond_to_app_agreement` | The side that didn't propose it |
| Sign | `sign_app_agreement`, or e-signature for program agreements | Both sides |
| End | `terminate_app_agreement` | Either side |
| Read | `list_app_agreements` | Both sides |

### Proposing from the app

`propose_app_agreement({ app_id, counterparty_entity_id, kind, scopes, products?, terms_summary, document_url?, document_sha256?, effective_from?, effective_to? })`

- `products` are ids of the app's own products.
- The document link must be https. Its SHA-256 (64 lowercase hex) is kept with it.
- The other firm is told: an `app_agreement.proposed` event on its webhooks and a notice to each member (`list_firm_notices`).

### Proposing from a licence provider

`propose_workspace_agreement({ workspace_id, app_id, kind, scopes, products?, terms_summary, document_url?, document_sha256?, template_id?, effective_from?, effective_to? })`

- `workspace_id` is the app's workspace.
- `kind` is `program`, `data_sharing`, `msa` or `sla`.
- A program agreement names the products the licence provider's firm sponsors for the app.
- `template_id` is one of its firm's agreement templates in use. A program agreement's e-signature document is then made from it, in place of the firm's most specific one.
- The app must use products the firm sponsors, or have an agreement with it already.
- The workspace's members' firms are told (`app_agreement.proposed`), and the workspace's attention list has an `app_agreement_proposed` item until the proposal is answered.

### Responding

`respond_to_app_agreement({ agreement_id, decision: "accept" | "decline", note? })` is called by the side that didn't propose:

- a member of the counterparty firm acting as its licence provider (with standing) or vendor; or
- the workspace's owners and admins.

The proposer can't answer its own proposal. It may withdraw it. Declining ends the agreement. When the app's side answers, the firm is told (`app_agreement.answered`).

### Signing

- Where e-signature is configured, program agreements are signed on the licence provider's own agreement (see [E-signature](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/agreements.md#e-signature)).
- Otherwise `sign_app_agreement({ agreement_id })` records one side's signature on an accepted agreement: the app's owners or admins for the app, a member of the other firm for the firm.

An agreement becomes `signed` only once both sides have signed. The other firm is then told (`app_agreement.signed`).

### Ending

`terminate_app_agreement({ agreement_id, reason })` is called by either side, on a proposed agreement (a withdrawal), an accepted one or a signed one. The other firm is told when the app's side ends it (`app_agreement.terminated`).

### Reading agreements

Every agreement in a reply names:

- its `scopes` (keys) and `scope_labels` (in words);
- `proposed_by_side`;
- the `template` it was made on: `{ id, name, version }` or `null`;
- `your_side`: `app`, `counterparty` or `both`;
- `actions`, what the caller may do now: `accept`, `decline`, `sign`, `withdraw`, `end`.

`list_app_agreements` has three forms. `status` and `scope` (one of the scope keys: only agreements covering it) filter any of them.

**`list_app_agreements({ app_id })`**, for any member of the app's workspace, returns:

- the app's agreements, each with both parties named, the products it covers, its status, signatures and effective dates;
- the products the app uses, each with its stage, the licence providers sponsoring it and the states they sponsor it in;
- the vendor services its workspace relies on: active subscriptions of its members' firms, each with the version of the vendor's standard terms accepted for this app and its `scopes` and `scope_labels` (`null` with no agreement for this app), or `no_standard_terms`;
- the introductions the connector has in progress for its members. The other side is named only once both have said yes. This is `null` when the connector doesn't run on this server.

**`list_app_agreements({ workspace_id })`**, for any member, returns every agreement of the workspace's apps (all kinds), `can_manage`, its apps, and `proposable_counterparties: [{ entity_id, name, product_ids, app_ids }]`: the licence providers sponsoring its apps' products.

**`list_app_agreements()`** with neither, for a licence provider or vendor, lists the agreements naming its firm, whichever side proposed them. A licence provider also gets `proposable_workspaces: [{ workspace: { id, name }, apps: [{ id, name, product_ids, sponsored_product_ids }] }]`.

### Audit and attention

Every change is audited with the app's id (and the workspace's) and the `side` that made it, in the obligations class: `propose_app_agreement`, `update_agreement_scopes`, `accept_app_agreement`, `decline_app_agreement`, `sign_app_agreement`, `terminate_app_agreement`, `accept_vendor_terms`.

The app's side hears of the other firm's answers, signatures and terminations in its workspace's attention list (`app_agreement_update`; see [The other firm's side in the attention list](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/agreements.md#the-other-firms-side-in-the-attention-list)).

`remove_app` refuses an app with agreements, which are the other firm's record too.

## Scopes

Every agreement records **one or more scopes**: what it covers, from a fixed list (`AGREEMENT_SCOPES` in `core/src/app-agreements-schema.ts`, which Mynt Studio shows by the same labels).

| Scope | Label | Covers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `technology` | Technology | A platform or software licence |
| `manpower` | Manpower | People and staffing |
| `financial_regulatory_operations` | Financial regulatory operations | Compliance and regulatory operations |

Rules:

- Both propose tools require `scopes`: at least one, each once, only from the list. Anything else is refused.
- The scopes are part of what the other side accepts and what is signed. An e-signature program schedule states them ("Scope of the agreement").
- Agreements made before scopes were recorded keep an empty list, which Studio shows as "Not set". Mynt never fills one in.
- `scope` filters find agreements by scope.

### Changing scopes

While an agreement is still `proposed`, the side that proposed it may change its scopes with `update_agreement_scopes({ agreement_id, scopes })`: the workspace's owners and admins for one their side proposed, a licence provider for one its firm proposed.

- Nothing else about the agreement changes.
- The change is audited (`update_agreement_scopes`, with `from_scopes` and `scopes`).
- The other side is told (`app_agreement.proposed` with `updated: "scopes"`).
- Once the proposal is answered, the scopes are fixed.

### Scopes on a vendor's standard terms

A vendor's standard terms carry scopes. A click-through agreement (`subscribe_vendor_service`) copies the scopes of the standard terms version accepted. Only one accepted on a terms version from before scopes were recorded has none ("Not set"). See [The marketplace and standard terms](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/vendors-and-marketplace.md#the-marketplace-and-standard-terms).

## Production needs program agreements

An app moves to `production` only with a **signed program agreement** with every licence provider sponsoring **each product it uses**, covering that product. This is the `program_agreements` promotion check. See [Stages and promotion](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/workspaces-and-sign-in.md#stages-and-promotion).

### Which licence providers

- Every licence provider with an approved sponsorship of the product counts, wherever it sponsors the product and whichever states the app serves.
- A product no licence provider sponsors is covered by its own firm's licences and needs no agreement.
- One agreement may cover several of the app's products from the same licence provider.
- A product with two sponsoring licence providers needs an agreement with each.

### In force

An agreement counts when:

- its `status` is `signed` (both sides signed);
- `effective_from` is unset, or on or before today;
- `effective_to` is unset, or today or later (the last day it runs).

A `vendor` or `data_sharing` agreement doesn't count.

### The check

`get_promotion_checks` gives it as `{ id: "program_agreements", label: "Signed program agreement with each product's sponsor", status, detail, fix?, coverage }`.

- Each missing pair fails the check in plain words: `No signed program agreement with <sponsor> for <product>`.
- Why the nearest agreement doesn't count follows in brackets. The reasons are:
  - `proposed, waiting for <sponsor> to accept`
  - `<sponsor> accepted it; waiting for your signature`
  - `its signed agreement takes effect on <date>`
  - `its signed agreement ended on <date>`
  - `it was ended on <date>: <reason>`
  - `<sponsor> declined it`
- `fix` is optional. It is `Propose agreement` (`propose_app_agreement`, the app's Agreements tab).
- `coverage` lists each pair: `{ product_id, product_name, sponsor_entity_id, sponsor_name, covered, agreement_id, agreement_status, note }`.
- With nothing to agree, the check passes as "Not applicable".

### The app's view

`list_app_agreements({ app_id })` also returns `program_coverage` (the same pairs) and `production_gate: { met, missing, flagged }`, with the app's `stage`.

### Ending after go-live

An agreement that is terminated or expires after the app reached production doesn't move the app back. The app keeps running, and:

- `production_gate.flagged` is true;
- its production checks fail, so the workspace's attention list has a `promotion_checks_failing` item naming the missing agreement;
- `ops_status` lists it under `apps.production_without_program_agreements` with an attention line.

There is no event channel to an app's workspace. App webhooks carry runtime events, whose list the generated SDKs pin. So the attention list is how the workspace hears of it.

### The other firm's side in the attention list

Each acceptance, decline, signature and termination by the other firm in the last 14 days is an `app_agreement_update` item in the workspace's attention list, linking to the app's Agreements tab.

| Priority | When |
| --- | --- |
| High | It ended a program agreement |
| Medium | Another agreement ended or was declined, or an agreement waits for an owner's or admin's signature |
| Low | Otherwise |

Where the agreement is signed by e-signature, the same list has:

- the other firm's signature on the document;
- the document completed, signed by both sides (low);
- the document declined at signing (medium);
- the document expired or cancelled at the service (high for a program agreement).

The `program_agreements` check's "waiting for your signature" or "waiting for <sponsor>'s signature" reads the document's signatures.

## Target customers

`get_app_customers({ app_id })`, for any member, lists:

- the customer segments (personas) each of the app's products declares (`customer_segments` in its definition);
- which ones the app targets;
- the app's customers where Mynt measures them: distinct customers with client sessions and with records in the customer vault, live and sandbox apart.

Without client sessions in an environment, its counts are `null` with the reason, never 0.

`set_app_target_segments({ app_id, segments: [{ product_id, segment_id }] })`, for owners and admins, replaces the app's choice. Each entry is a segment its product declares. It is audited as `set_app_target_segments`.

## E-signature

Where e-signature is configured, a program agreement is signed on the licence provider's own agreement, by both parties, through an e-signature service, and Mynt keeps the signed copy.

- The core is brand-neutral (`core/src/esign/provider.ts`).
- Each service is an adapter (`core/src/esign/signwell.ts`) chosen by a setting.
- The flow is in `core/src/agreement-esign.ts`.

Every kind except `program` (`vendor`, `data_sharing`, `msa` and `sla`) keeps the manual `sign_app_agreement` flow, whether or not e-signature is configured.

### Agreement templates

A licence provider's members upload their firm's program agreement once, and Mynt uses it for every app that signs with them. Only the firm's own licence providers (with standing) manage its templates. A Mynt admin can't act for them.

| Tool | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `upload_agreement_template` | Adds a template or the next version of one |
| `list_agreement_templates` | The firm's templates (`include_retired` for older versions), never the file |
| `retire_agreement_template` | Stops using a version for new agreements. Documents made from it are unaffected |

`upload_agreement_template` takes `{ name, source?: "upload" | "provider_template", licence_id? | sponsorship_id?, file_name?, file_base64?, provider_template_id?, placeholders?, field_map?, signature_placement?, notes? }`.

- **An upload** is a PDF or DOCX, checked by its bytes, at most 5 MB. It is sealed with `MYNT_VAULT_KEY` and kept with its SHA-256.
- **A provider template** is the id of a template the firm keeps at the e-signature service, with the names of its two signer placeholders (`counterparty`, `app`) and a `field_map` from Mynt's variables to the template's field ids.
- Mynt's variables are `licence_provider`, `developer_firm`, `app`, `products`, `states`, `effective_from`, `effective_to`, `agreement_id`, `terms_summary` and `scope`.
- Attach the template to one of the firm's licences or sponsorships, or to neither for the firm's default.
- `signature_placement` is `signature_page` (a signature page added at the end, the default) or `text_tags` (the file carries the service's text tags).
- Versions never change. The same name again is the next version, and the active one.

### The signing flow

1. **Propose and accept.** Either side proposes the program agreement and the other accepts it, as in [App agreements](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/agreements.md#app-agreements).
2. **Mynt makes the document.** On acceptance, Mynt picks the template: the one the licence provider proposed the agreement on (`template_id`) while it is still in use, else the firm's most specific active template. Most specific means one attached to an approved sponsorship of the agreement's products, else to a licence those sponsorships are approved under, else the firm's default.
3. **Mynt appends its program schedule**, a PDF stating what Mynt fills in: both parties, the builder's firm, the app, the products, the scope (its scopes in words, or "Not set"), the states the sponsorship covers, the dates, the agreement's id, and the template's version and SHA-256.
4. **Two signers.** Mynt creates the e-signature document with two signers: whoever acted for the licence provider (accepted the agreement, or proposed it) and whoever acted for the app. They sign in either order.
5. **Each signer opens a signing page.** `get_agreement_signing_link({ agreement_id })` gives the signer on the caller's side an embedded signing page, which Studio opens in a sheet. Only that signer gets it, and it is asked for afresh each time. Mynt never stores it.
6. **The service reports back.** See [The e-signature webhook](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/agreements.md#the-e-signature-webhook).
7. **Both sides download.** `download_agreement_document({ agreement_id, part?: "signed" | "certificate" })` returns the file as base64 with its SHA-256, checked against the recorded hash. Only members of either party can read it: the app's workspace, or the other firm.

If the firm has no template yet, or the service can't be reached, the agreement stays `accepted`. The document is made the first time a signer asks to sign.

### The e-signature webhook

The service's webhook (`POST <PUBLIC_URL>/esign/webhook`) is checked against the service's own scheme with the raw body and a constant-time compare.

- Events older than three days are refused.
- Each event is handled once.
- An event only prompts Mynt to read the document's state back from the service, because the service's signature doesn't cover the document an event names.
- Opening a signing link or a signed copy reads the state too.

### What signed means

Only a document the service reports completed, with both signers signed, signs the agreement. Mynt then:

1. downloads the signed copy, and the same with the service's audit certificate (who signed, when and from where);
2. seals both with `MYNT_VAULT_KEY`;
3. records each SHA-256 (the signed copy's becomes the agreement's `document_sha256`);
4. sets the agreement `signed` with `signed_at`.

Other outcomes:

- A signer declining makes the agreement `declined`.
- The document cancelled or expired ends it (`terminated`).
- Ending an agreement whose document is still out cancels the document at the service.

With e-signature configured, `sign_app_agreement` refuses program agreements. Without it, the manual flow is how both sides record their signatures.

### What the tools and the audit trail show

`list_app_agreements` shows each program agreement's `signed_by_esignature` and `signature_document`: its status, test mode, template, whether each side has signed, and the signed copy's hashes.

Every step is audited, in the obligations class: `upload_agreement_template`, `retire_agreement_template`, `esign_document_created`, `esign_document_failed`, `open_agreement_signing`, `esign_signer_signed`, `esign_completed`, `esign_declined`, `esign_canceled`, `esign_expired`, `download_agreement_document`.

### Setting it up in Mynt Studio

Nobody edits the server's environment. A Mynt admin opens **Platform admin → Platform settings** (`/platform/settings`; see [Platform settings](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/platform-admin.md#platform-settings)) and does the rest in its E-signature tab. The old workspace **Settings → E-signature** address goes there.

1. **Save the key.** Press **Set key**, pick the service (`signwell`), paste its API key into the sheet's password field and press **Check and save key**. Mynt checks the key with a cheap authenticated read of the key's own account. A key the service refuses isn't kept. An accepted key is kept in the [platform key vault](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/platform-admin.md#the-key-vault): sealed by the confidential host in Mynt's database (`platform_secrets`, one row per key). It is never returned, shown or logged: the tab shows only "Key set on <date> by <admin>". The key is a row of the Key vault tab too, and **Set key** there does the same.
2. **Mynt registers the webhook.** It registers the service's webhook to `<PUBLIC_URL>/esign/webhook`, reusing one already pointing there, and seals the webhook's id the same way. The service signs its events with that id (HMAC-SHA256 of the event's `type@time`). **Re-register webhook** does this again. Without an https `PUBLIC_URL` the key is kept, and the tab says the webhook waits for one.
3. **Choose the mode.** **Change mode** opens a sheet with the **Test mode** switch, on by default. On: documents are free and not legally binding, for trying the whole flow. Off: documents are legally binding and count towards the service's billing. Documents already made keep the mode they were made in.
4. **Remove the key, when needed.** **Remove key** (typed out to confirm) deletes the webhook at the service, then retires the stored key and webhook id and destroys their values. Program agreements are then signed by hand.

The tab is one table. Its rows are whether e-signature is on, the key's line, the mode, whether the webhook is registered, and when Mynt last received an event.

### E-signature admin tools

The tools behind the tab are `get_esign_settings`, `set_esign_api_key`, `register_esign_webhook`, `remove_esign_api_key` and `set_esign_test_mode`. They are for Mynt admins only and never return a secret.

They are audited in the security class without any value: `set_esign_api_key`, `set_esign_api_key_refused`, `register_esign_webhook`, `register_esign_webhook_refused`, `remove_esign_api_key` and `set_esign_test_mode`.

### Environment overrides

Where set, these settings win over what is stored, so a deployment that set them keeps working. Names only:

| Setting | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `ESIGN_PROVIDER` | The adapter (`signwell`), over the stored choice |
| `SIGNWELL_API_KEY` | Secret. Over the stored key |
| `SIGNWELL_WEBHOOK_ID` | Secret. Over the stored webhook id |
| `ESIGN_TEST_MODE` | `off` for live documents, over the switch |
| `MYNT_VAULT_KEY` | Required to keep the key, the webhook id, templates and signed copies |

Without a key anywhere, e-signature is off. The tools then say "E-signature isn't configured on this deployment yet" and the manual flow stays.

### The signing frame

- The adapter lists the origins the service's signing pages come from.
- `get_agreement_signing_link` says whether the link's origin is one of them (`signing_origin_allowed`).
- Mynt publishes the list at `GET /esign/frame-origins`, which is public, names no secret, and is empty while e-signature is off.
- Studio reads it every few minutes and allows exactly those origins in its Content-Security-Policy `frame-src`, so the Sign sheet frames the signing page.
- `ESIGN_FRAME_SRC` (Studio's setting) can add origins.
- A link from anywhere else is offered in a new tab instead.

## Oversight audits

A program agreement also says which **oversight audits** its licence provider runs on the app: an annual compliance review, a quarterly complaints review, a review of the marketing material on each change.

An agreement has many audit requirements. Each requirement has many audits over time, one open at a time.

The tools are in `core/src/agreement-audits.ts`. The tables (`agreement_audit_requirements`, `agreement_audits`) are in `core/src/agreement-audits-schema.ts`.

These audits are the agreement's own, not the regulator's. The regulatory obligations under `get_workspace_obligations` keep their register's schema and aren't changed by them.

### Audit requirements

A requirement is managed by a licence provider: a member of the agreement's counterparty firm with licence-provider standing.

`add_agreement_audit_requirement({ agreement_id, name, kind, cadence, first_due?, description?, evidence_required? })` adds one to a `program` agreement that is proposed, accepted or signed. So requirements can come with the licence provider's terms before it signs.

| Field | Values |
| --- | --- |
| `kind` | `compliance_review`, `complaints_review`, `marketing_review`, `security_review`, `financial_review`, `other` |
| `cadence` | `once`, `monthly`, `quarterly`, `annual`, `on_change` |
| `first_due` | YYYY-MM-DD. Required except for `on_change`, which has none |

At most 50 live requirements per agreement.

`retire_agreement_audit_requirement({ requirement_id, reason })` stops one. Its open audit is waived with that reason, and closed ones stay.

### Scheduling

Audits run only under a signed agreement. A timer (every minute, `sweepAgreementAudits`), and each add and close, opens a requirement's next audit (`scheduled`) when it has none open.

| Cadence | Next audit |
| --- | --- |
| `once` | One audit, due on `first_due` |
| `monthly`, `quarterly`, `annual` | Due on `first_due`, then a month, three months or a year after the previous one's due date (the day clamped to the month's end). It opens 14, 30 or 60 days before it is due |
| `on_change` | Opens when the app's builds give it new verified source: a succeeded build whose source SHA-256 differs from the one the last audit was opened for. Due 30 days later. The licence provider can also open one by hand |

Mynt can't tell which files customers see, so every new verified source counts as a change.

A due date runs to the end of its day, UTC.

### An audit's life

An audit is `scheduled`, `in_progress`, `submitted`, then `passed`, `failed` or `waived`.

| Tool | Who | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `open_agreement_audit({ audit_id })` | Licence provider | Opens a scheduled audit. It is in progress and the caller is its reviewer |
| `open_agreement_audit({ requirement_id, due? })` | Licence provider | Opens one by hand, due on `due` or 30 days from now. Refused while that requirement has one open |
| `submit_agreement_audit_evidence({ audit_id, evidence: [{ name, url, sha256 }], note? })` | The app's workspace owners and admins | Adds evidence. The audit becomes `submitted` |
| `record_agreement_audit_finding({ audit_id, severity, title, detail? })` | Licence provider | Adds an open finding and sends a scheduled or submitted audit back to `in_progress`. `severity` is `low`, `medium`, `high` or `critical` |
| `respond_to_agreement_audit_finding({ audit_id, finding_id, response })` | Owners and admins | Answers a finding |
| `resolve_agreement_audit_finding({ audit_id, finding_id, note? })` | Licence provider | Resolves a finding |
| `close_agreement_audit({ audit_id, outcome, note? })` | Licence provider | Closes the audit |

Evidence is https links with their SHA-256. Mynt keeps links and hashes, not files. At most 20 at a time and 50 per audit.

Closing: `passed` only once the audit is `submitted` and every finding is resolved; `failed` or `waived` at any point, with a note saying why. The requirement's next audit then opens when its time comes.

### Reading audits

Only the agreement's two parties read its audits: any member of the app's workspace, and the counterparty firm's licence providers.

`list_agreement_audits({ workspace_id?, app_id?, agreement_id?, status?, overdue?, side? })` returns `{ requirements, audits, counts: { audits, open, overdue } }`:

- each requirement with its counterparty, how many audits it has had, its next due date and whether it is overdue;
- each audit with its requirement, agreement, app and counterparty, `overdue`, `findings_open`, `your_side` and `actions`.

`actions` is what the caller may do next: `open`, `record_finding`, `resolve_finding`, `pass`, `fail`, `waive`, `submit_evidence`, `respond_to_finding`.

`get_agreement_audit({ audit_id })` adds the people named and its `history`: every audit-log entry for it, who made it and when. The schedule's own entries have no actor.

### Overdue audits

Overdue means past its due date and not closed. A submitted audit waiting for review still counts.

An overdue audit flags the app:

- `get_workspace_attention` lists it as `agreement_audit_overdue`;
- `ops_status` counts overdue audits and the apps they are on (`agreement_audits`);
- the lists mark it.

### Audit trail and events for oversight audits

Every change is audited with the app's id, in the obligations class: `add_agreement_audit_requirement`, `retire_agreement_audit_requirement`, `agreement_audit_scheduled`, `open_agreement_audit`, `submit_agreement_audit_evidence`, `record_agreement_audit_finding`, `respond_to_agreement_audit_finding`, `resolve_agreement_audit_finding`, `pass_agreement_audit`, `fail_agreement_audit`, `waive_agreement_audit`.

Both parties' firms are told on their webhooks and notices:

| Event | When |
| --- | --- |
| `agreement_audit.opened` | Opened by the schedule or the licence provider |
| `agreement_audit.submitted` | Evidence or an answer from the app's side |
| `agreement_audit.closed` | Closed, with its outcome |

## Service levels

A service-level agreement (an app agreement of kind `sla`) carries **commitments**: API uptime of 99.9% a month, complaints answered within two business days.

One SLA agreement has many commitments. Each commitment has **breaches** over time: a period in which the measured value missed the target.

The tables are `agreement_slas` and `agreement_sla_breaches` (`core/src/agreement-slas-schema.ts`). The tools are in `core/src/agreement-slas.ts`.

Either party may act: the counterparty firm's licence providers, or the workspace's owners and admins. Plain members read only.

### Service-level tools

**`add_agreement_sla({ agreement_id, metric, target, unit?, measurement_window, measurement_source, remedy? })`** adds a commitment to an `sla` agreement while it is `proposed` or `accepted`. Returns `{ sla }`.

- `target` is a number or words. A numeric one is also kept as `target_value`.
- `measurement_window` is `daily`, `weekly`, `monthly` or `quarterly`.
- `measurement_source` says where the measured value comes from.
- `remedy` says what happens when the target is missed.
- At most 50 active commitments per agreement.
- There is no separate acceptance of each commitment. They are the agreement's terms, in force once it is signed.

**`retire_agreement_sla({ sla_id, reason })`** stops a commitment while the agreement is open. Its breaches stay, and open ones can still be resolved. Returns `{ sla }`.

**`record_sla_breach({ sla_id, period_start, period_end, measured_value, note? })`** records a missed period on an active commitment of a signed agreement. Returns `{ breach, sla }`. The breach says which side recorded it (`recorded_side`).

**`resolve_sla_breach({ breach_id, note? })`** closes an open breach. Returns `{ breach }`.

**`list_agreement_slas({ workspace_id?, app_id?, agreement_id?, side?, include_retired? })`** is for both parties, scoped as `list_agreement_audits` is, over `sla` agreements only. It returns `{ agreements, slas, counts: { slas, active, open_breaches } }`:

- each agreement with its app, workspace, counterparty, `your_side` and `can_add_slas`;
- each commitment with its app, counterparty, `open_breaches`, its `breaches` and its `actions` (`record_breach`, `retire`);
- each breach is `open` or resolved, with who recorded it and its own `actions` (`resolve`).

### Open breaches

An open breach flags the app:

- `get_workspace_attention` lists it as `agreement_sla_breach`;
- `ops_status` counts open breaches and the agreements they are on (`sla_breaches: { open, agreements }`).

Every change is audited with the app's and workspace's ids, in the obligations class: `add_agreement_sla`, `retire_agreement_sla`, `record_sla_breach`, `resolve_sla_breach`.

A breach is told to both parties' firms on their webhooks and notices: `agreement_sla.breached`, with the commitment, the metric and target, the measured value, the period and the side that recorded it.

## Agreements in Studio

Agreements appear in three places in Mynt Studio: an app's **Agreements** tab, the **Licences** page and the **Audits** page. See [Licences](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/studio.md#licences) and [Audits](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/studio.md#audits) for the pages as a whole.

### The app's Agreements tab

- It lists what production needs: each licence provider and product, signed and in force or why not. Owners and admins get a **Propose agreement** shortcut pre-filled with that licence provider and product.
- It flags an app in production that lost an agreement.
- Each agreement row has labelled actions for owners and admins, each opening a sheet:

| Action | When |
| --- | --- |
| **Accept**, **Decline** | A proposal the other firm made |
| **Sign** | Accepted, your side not signed yet |
| **Withdraw** | Your own proposal, with a reason |
| **End agreement** | Accepted or signed, with a reason |

The app's **Products** tab and the **Promote to Production** sheet show the `program_agreements` check with the same rows and shortcut.

### The Licences page

The Licences page (`/licences?tab=business-agreements|msa|sla|audit-obligations`) is where both sides work on their agreements. It is in the sidebar for builders and for licence providers, even without the builder role.

It has four tabs in the page body under the header: **Business Agreements**, **MSA**, **SLA** and **Audit Obligations**. Each lists what the person's side holds:

- a licence provider sees the agreements made with its firm;
- a builder sees its selected workspace's (`list_app_agreements` with `workspace_id`);
- someone who is both sees both, each row saying its side.

The page has no row of figures and no licence table or coverage map. Licence coverage is on each product's **Compliance** tab. `/coverage`, `/licences?view=map` and the old `?tab=coverage` come back to `/licences`, and `?tab=agreements` is Business Agreements.

**Business Agreements, MSA and SLA.** Business Agreements holds program and data-sharing agreements, MSA master services agreements and SLA service-level agreements. Each is a table with:

- columns for the app, the other party, products, kind, scope, status in words, effective dates, document and actions;
- a full-width search, a Filters popover (status, kind where the tab has more than one, scope, and your side when you are on both) and a Proposed date range;
- **Import** (disabled: agreements are made here) and **Export CSV**;
- the tab's own **Propose agreement**, **Propose MSA** or **Propose SLA**.

Either side proposes, for one app, MSAs and SLAs too: a builder to a firm sponsoring the app's products, a licence provider to a workspace whose app builds on them. A licence provider may start from one of its templates. The other side uses **Accept** or **Decline**. While the proposal is still proposed, the proposer may **Withdraw** it or use **Change scope** (`update_agreement_scopes`) to change what it covers. Then both **Sign**. **End agreement** ends it.

**Review agreement.** A row opens **Review agreement**: a card with the terms and the document, the labelled actions for the row's side, then tabs, each a table.

| Tab | On | Shows | Actions |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Products** | Every agreement | The products it covers | |
| **Signatures** | Every agreement | Who signed | |
| **Commitments** | An SLA | Metric, target, window, source, remedy, status | **Add commitment** before it is signed; **Record breach** and **Retire commitment** on each |
| **Breaches** | An SLA | Period, measured value, who recorded it, status | **Resolve breach** |

A licence provider also has **Add audit requirement** on an open program agreement of its firm.

**Agreement templates.** Under the MSA table, a licence provider has its firm's **Agreement templates**: name, version, attached to, file, SHA-256, in use or retired. **Upload agreement template** opens a sheet (name, licence, file, signature placement, field placement notes), and **Retire** retires a version.

**Audit Obligations.** This tab shows the oversight audits under program agreements (`list_agreement_audits`): requirement, agreement, app, kind, cadence, due date, status in words with Overdue, and findings. It only shows them, and so does an audit's sheet there.

### The Audits page

Oversight audits are acted on from the **Audits** page's **Agreement audits** tab.

### Signing in Studio with e-signature

With [e-signature](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/agreements.md#e-signature) configured, **Sign** on a program agreement opens the signer's embedded signing page in a sheet instead of recording a signature by hand. Once both have signed, each side's row offers **Download signed copy** and **Download certificate**.

pages.title: Risk
pages.markdown:
This file covers the risk registers kept for apps, for financial products and for Mynt itself, how each risk is scored in three steps and graded, what a risk holds under it (factors, treatment tasks, controls and links), the seven risk areas, and Mynt's own risk models. It is for builders, who keep the registers of their apps and products, and for Mynt admins, who keep the platform's register and its risk models.

See also: [Agreements](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/agreements.md), [Products](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/products.md), [Workspaces and sign-in](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/workspaces-and-sign-in.md), [Platform administration](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/platform-admin.md), [Mynt Studio](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/studio.md).

## Risk registers

Apps and financial products each keep a risk register of the same shape, and so does Mynt itself (the platform's own register). A register says what could go wrong, how likely it is and how bad it would be, who owns it, what is being done about it and when it is next looked at.

### What a risk holds

| Field | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `title`, `description` | The risk in words |
| `category` | One of the nine risk categories: `security`, `fraud`, `vendor`, `conduct`, `operational`, `compliance`, `credit`, `liquidity` or `other` |
| `risk_area` | One of the seven [risk areas](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/risk.md#risk-areas). Required on Mynt's own register. Elsewhere it is its category's by default. Null is unassigned |
| `likelihood`, `impact` | 1 to 5 each |
| `inherent` | The inherent score: likelihood times impact, with its `level` and `level_name`. `score` and `level` at the top of the risk are the same two |
| `control` | How well the risk's controls work: `effectiveness` (`none`, `weak`, `partial`, `strong`, or null: not assessed), `words` and a `note` |
| `residual` | The residual score with its `level` and `level_name`, whether it is `assessed`, whether it is `overridden`, and `words` saying which. See [Scoring in three steps](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/risk.md#scoring-in-three-steps) |
| `owner` | A member of the app's workspace, or of the product's firm. By default, whoever adds the risk |
| `mitigation` | What is being done about it |
| `status` | `open`, `mitigating`, `accepted` or `closed` |
| `review_by` | The date it is next reviewed by. Past it, and not closed, the risk is `overdue` |

### Scoring in three steps

Every risk on every register is scored the same way.

1. **Inherent.** Likelihood times impact, 1 to 25: the risk before anything is done about it. Its level comes from the inherent bands.
2. **Control.** How well the risk's controls work together, in four steps: `none`, `weak`, `partial` or `strong`. Until someone says, the control is not assessed.
3. **Residual.** What is left after the controls. Mynt derives it from the inherent score and the control step by the platform's [risk grading](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/risk.md#risk-grading), and grades it by the residual bands.

Two cases are said in words, never as a blank or a 0:

- **Not assessed.** A risk whose control isn't assessed has no derived residual. Its residual is its inherent score, `residual.assessed` is false, and the words say "same as inherent, control not assessed". Risks made before three-step scoring are in this state until they are reviewed.
- **Overridden.** A keeper may set the residual likelihood and impact themselves (`update_risk` with `residual_likelihood`, `residual_impact` and `residual_override_reason`). Their product is the residual score. Who set it, when and why are kept, and a change to the grading never derives it again. `clear_residual_override: true` goes back to the derived score.

### Who keeps which register

A register's subject (`subject_type`) is `app`, `product` or `platform`.

| Register | Adds and reviews risks | Reads it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| An app's | Its workspace's owners and admins | Any member of its workspace |
| A financial product's | Its own firm: the product's owner, or a builder at the firm it belongs to | Its firm, and the licence providers sponsoring it (an approved sponsorship), read-only |
| Mynt's own (`subject_type: "platform"`, `subject_id: "mynt"`) | Mynt admins | Mynt admins only. To anyone else it doesn't exist |

### Register tools

**`add_risk({ subject_type: "app" | "product" | "platform", subject_id, title, category, risk_area?, likelihood, impact, description?, mitigation?, owner_user_id?, review_by?, control_effectiveness?, control_note? })`** adds a risk, `open`. `risk_area` is required for `platform`. Without `control_effectiveness` the control is not assessed.

**`update_risk({ risk_id, status?, risk_area?, mitigation?, likelihood?, impact?, owner_user_id?, review_by?, control_effectiveness?, control_note?, residual_likelihood?, residual_impact?, residual_override_reason?, clear_residual_override?, note? })`** reviews a risk. Only what is passed changes. Accepting or closing a risk needs a `note` saying why. An override needs all three of its fields.

**`list_risks({ subject_type, subject_id, status?, category?, risk_area?, residual_level?, overdue_only?, risk_id? })`** lists the register, highest residual score first, with:

- each risk's three scores (`inherent`, `control`, `residual`), each level in words;
- counts by status and of overdue reviews, and `residual_levels`: the risks not yet closed, by the level of their residual score;
- `level_names`: the platform's name for each level;
- `can_manage`: whether the caller may add and review.

`risk_area` is one area, or `unassigned` for risks with none. `residual_level` is `low`, `medium`, `high` or `critical`. With `risk_id`, the reply is that risk and its history; `get_risk` returns the same history with everything under the risk.

**`admin_list_risks({ limit?, subject_type?, risk_area?, residual_level? })`**, for Mynt admins, reads every register's risks that aren't closed: apps', products' and the platform's, or one kind, or one risk area, or `unassigned`. It returns:

- `counts` by inherent level and `residual_counts` by residual level (`critical`, `high`, `medium`, `low`), how many are overdue, and the total;
- the risks, highest residual score first, then by inherent score, then by review date, each with its three scores;
- for each risk, its `subject_name` and where it lives: `workspace_id` for an app's, `firm_id` for a product's, null for a reference product.

### One risk in full

**`get_risk({ risk_id })`** returns one risk with everything under it. Whoever reads the register reads it. Mynt admins also read any app's or product's risk this way, and never write it (`can_manage` is false).

| Part | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `risk` | The risk, with its three scores |
| `scoring` | Three lists of factors, `impact`, `likelihood` and `control`. Each has the score it explains (`recorded`), the factors' `average` (null when there are none), its `formula` in words and the `factors` |
| `treatments`, `treatment_due` | The treatment tasks, and the earliest due date among the open ones (null when none has one) |
| `controls` | The controls, retired ones included |
| `links` | What the risk is about |
| `history` | Every change, oldest first: when, who, what changed in words, the note, and the scores before and after (`score.before`, `score.after`, each `{ inherent, control, residual }`) |

A history entry from before three-step scoring carries the inherent score only. Its residual is null, "not recorded", never a guess.

### Factors, treatment tasks, controls and links

These are kept by whoever keeps the register, with the same rules as the register itself. Each write names the risk (`risk_id`).

**Factors** explain the three scores. They don't set them: the risk's likelihood, impact and control effectiveness change only with `update_risk`.

| Field | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `kind` | `impact`, `likelihood` or `control`: which score it explains |
| `name`, `rationale` | The factor in words, and why it scores as it does |
| `score` | 1 to 5. For impact and likelihood, as the risk's own. For a control factor, 1 is not working and 5 is working fully |
| `source` | Where it comes from: an `https` link, or something on Mynt as `type:id` (the types are the link targets below) |

- **`add_risk_factor({ risk_id, kind, name, score, rationale?, source? })`**
- **`update_risk_factor({ risk_id, factor_id, name?, score?, rationale?, source? })`**
- **`remove_risk_factor({ risk_id, factor_id })`**. The audit trail keeps what the factor was.

**Treatment tasks** are the work that brings the risk down.

| Field | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `title`, `owner`, `due` | The task, who owns it (someone on the register's side; by default whoever adds it) and when it is due. Past its due date and still open, it is `overdue` |
| `status` | `todo`, `doing`, `done` or `dropped`. Marking it done records `done_at` |
| `progress_note` | Where it stands, in words |
| `effectiveness`, `effectiveness_note` | Whether it worked: `not_assessed`, `ineffective`, `partly_effective` or `effective`. Saying it worked or didn't needs the task done |

- **`add_risk_treatment({ risk_id, title, owner_user_id?, due?, progress_note? })`**
- **`update_risk_treatment({ risk_id, treatment_id, title?, owner_user_id?, due?, status?, progress_note?, effectiveness?, effectiveness_note? })`**

**Controls** are what keeps the risk down. A control records what is in place; how well the controls work together is the risk's control effectiveness.

| Field | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `name`, `description` | The control and what it does |
| `kind` | `preventive` (stops it happening), `detective` (notices it) or `corrective` (puts it right) |
| `last_tested_at`, `test_result` | When it was last tested (not in the future) and the result: `passed`, `gaps_found` or `failed`. Null is not tested |
| `from_treatment` | The treatment task it was made from, when it was |
| `retired` | When and why it was retired. A retired control stays listed and can't be changed |

- **`add_risk_control({ risk_id, name?, kind, description?, last_tested_at?, test_result?, source_treatment_id? })`**. With `source_treatment_id`, the control is made from one of the risk's treatment tasks that is done, once, and takes the task's title unless a name is given.
- **`update_risk_control({ risk_id, control_id, name?, kind?, description?, last_tested_at?, test_result? })`**
- **`retire_risk_control({ risk_id, control_id, reason })`**

**Links** say what the risk is about.

| `target_type` | What it points at |
| --- | --- |
| `app`, `product`, `firm` | An app, a financial product or a firm |
| `vendor_offering` | A vendor's service |
| `agreement`, `agreement_audit` | An app's agreement, or an oversight audit under one |
| `audit_entry` | An audit-trail entry |
| `risk_model` | One of Mynt's risk models. Mynt admins only |

- **`link_risk({ risk_id, target_type, target_id, note? })`**. One link per risk and item.
- **`unlink_risk({ risk_id, link_id })`**

You can link what you can read: your own apps, products and firm, published products, listed vendor services, your agreements and their audits. A link's `name` is returned only to someone who may read what it points at. To anyone else it is null, the same whether the item exists or not.

## Risk grading

How risks are graded is one platform setting, `risk_grading`, read and changed by Mynt admins only. It holds:

| Part | What it holds | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `levels` | The name of each of the four levels (`low`, `medium`, `high`, `critical`) | Low, Medium, High, Critical |
| `inherent_bands` | The inherent score's band for each level, `{ level, from, to }` | 1-4 low, 5-9 medium, 10-14 high, 15-25 critical |
| `residual_bands` | The residual score's bands, the same way | The same as the inherent bands |
| `residual_method` | `reduce` or `matrix` | `reduce` |
| `reduce` | For `reduce`: the share of the inherent score each control step takes away, 0 to 1 | none 0, weak 0.25, partial 0.5, strong 0.75 |
| `matrix` | For `matrix`: the residual level for each inherent level and control step | No control and a weak one leave the level; a partial one takes it one level down, a strong one two |

The two residual methods:

- **`reduce`:** residual = inherent × (1 − the step's reduction), rounded to the nearest whole number and never below 1. An inherent 20 with a partial control is 10.
- **`matrix`:** the inherent level and the control step pick a residual level. The residual score is the top of that level's residual band, or the inherent score when that is lower.

A grading is refused unless:

- each set of bands is the four levels in order, contiguous, starting at 1 and ending at 25;
- each level has its own name;
- a stronger control never reduces less than a weaker one, and no matrix cell is above its inherent level (a control never raises a risk).

**`get_risk_grading()`** returns the grading in force and its `version` (0 means Mynt's defaults, never changed), the method in words, the 5×5 likelihood × impact grid with each cell's score and level (`heat_map`), the defaults, and every version kept, newest first.

**`set_risk_grading({ levels?, inherent_bands?, residual_bands?, residual_method?, reduce?, matrix?, restore_version?, note })`** changes it, saying why. Pass what changes, or `restore_version` to bring back a kept version's content. Either way:

- it becomes a new version, and every earlier one is kept (the first change keeps Mynt's defaults as version 1);
- every residual score whose control is assessed and that isn't overridden is derived again;
- the audit trail records how many moved (`set_risk_grading`, with `residuals_changed`), and each moved risk's own history shows it (`rederive_risk_residual`).

### Signals around an app

For an app, `list_risks` also returns `signals`, what Mynt measures around it. Each is `{ available: true, rows }`, or `{ available: false, reason }` when Mynt doesn't measure it. It is never an empty list in its place.

| Signal | Rows |
| --- | --- |
| `fraud` | Not measured yet. Mynt records no fraud or velocity signals from customer sessions |
| `vendors` | The workspace's vendor services whose latest conformance run failed, whose calls mostly erred over the last 7 days, or whose subscription ended in the last 90 days; and the app's vendor contracts that were ended or ran out |
| `conduct` | Findings still open in the oversight audits licence providers run under the app's agreements, for requirements of the `marketing_review` and `complaints_review` kinds (see [Oversight audits](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/agreements.md#oversight-audits)) |
| `products` | The app's products with new sales paused by a licence provider's covenant, or drifted from their published composition |

### Audit and operations

- Every change is audited with the app's or product's id, in the obligations class, so it shows in the app's audit trail: `add_risk` and `update_risk`, and against the same risk `add_risk_factor`, `update_risk_factor`, `remove_risk_factor`, `add_risk_treatment`, `update_risk_treatment`, `add_risk_control`, `update_risk_control`, `retire_risk_control`, `link_risk` and `unlink_risk`. That trail is the risk's history.
- `ops_status` counts risks whose review date has passed and that aren't closed (`risks.overdue_reviews`), and says so under what needs attention. Overdue reviews of the platform's risks count with the others'.
- `remove_app` removes the app's register with it, and what each risk holds under it (factors, treatment tasks, controls and links). Each risk's history stays in the audit trail. A link from another register's risk to the removed app stays, without a name.

## Risk areas

The platform groups risk into seven risk areas. Every risk on a register may carry one (`risk_area`), and every risk model has one. An area is also the tab a risk or a model shows under in the platform admin.

| `risk_area` | Label |
| --- | --- |
| `financial` | Financial risk |
| `compliance` | Compliance risk |
| `third_party` | Third-party risk |
| `operations` | Operations risk |
| `business_process` | Business process risk |
| `technology` | Technology risk |
| `regulated_product` | Regulated product risk |

### How categories map to areas

A risk's `category` stays as it was given. Its `risk_area` is the platform's coarser grouping.

When no area is given, the risk takes its category's. Risks made before risk areas existed were filled in the same way, once, when the server starts.

| `category` | `risk_area` |
| --- | --- |
| `credit`, `liquidity` | `financial` |
| `compliance`, `conduct` | `compliance` |
| `vendor` | `third_party` |
| `operational`, `fraud` | `operations` |
| `security` | `technology` |
| `other` | None: unassigned until a review gives it one |

No category maps to `business_process` or `regulated_product`. A risk is in one of those areas only when the area is given.

## Risk models
