Mynt keeps its own risk models: how the platform measures each of its seven risk areas. They are kept and read by Mynt admins only. To anyone else the tools don't exist.

A financial product's own risk models stay in its definition (`risk_models`; see [Product definitions](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/products.md#product-definitions)).

### What a risk model holds

| Field | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `risk_area` | One of the seven: `financial`, `compliance`, `third_party`, `operations`, `business_process`, `technology`, `regulated_product` |
| `name`, `purpose` | What it is and what it is for |
| `method` | The formula or approach, in words |
| `inputs` | A list of `{ name, description?, source? }` |
| `outputs` | The scores or measures it produces: a list of `{ name, description? }` |
| `thresholds` | A list of `{ name, value, meaning? }`: the level (a number or words) and what happens at or beyond it |
| `owner` | A Mynt admin. By default, whoever adds it |
| `status` | `draft`, `active` or `retired` |
| `version` | Starts at 1. Each change to what the model is (name, purpose, method, inputs, outputs, thresholds) adds a version and never changes an old one |
| `validation` | The last one (`last_validated_at`, `validated_by`, `outcome`, `notes`), `next_validation_due`, and `overdue` once that date has passed on a model that isn't retired |
| `health`, `health_words` | Derived, in words. See below |
| `linked_risks` | How many risks on registers link to it (`link_risk` with `target_type: "risk_model"`) |

A validation's `outcome` is `passed`, `passed_with_findings` or `failed`.

A model's health is the first of these that holds:

| `health` | In words | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `retired` | Retired | The model is retired. It is never counted as unhealthy |
| `last_validation_failed` | Last validation failed | Its last validation's outcome is `failed` |
| `validation_overdue` | Validation overdue | Its next validation date has passed |
| `no_validation_yet` | No validation yet | It has never been validated |
| `healthy` | Healthy | None of the above |

### Risk model tools

**`add_risk_model({ risk_area, name, purpose, method, inputs?, outputs?, thresholds?, owner_user_id?, status?: "draft" | "active", next_validation_due? })`** adds a model at version 1, `draft` by default.

**`update_risk_model({ model_id, name?, purpose?, method?, inputs?, outputs?, thresholds?, owner_user_id?, status?, next_validation_due?, note? })`** changes a model that isn't retired.

- A change to what it is adds a version. The rest is carried over, and `note` is kept as its change note.
- Owner, status and due date change on the model itself.

**`validate_risk_model({ model_id, outcome, notes, next_validation_due })`** records a validation of the current version. Every one is kept. A failed one doesn't change the status.

**`retire_risk_model({ model_id, reason })`** retires a model. It stays listed with its history, can't be changed or validated, and is never overdue.

**`list_risk_models({ risk_area?, status?, model_id? })`** lists the models, newest first, with counts by status, of overdue validations and of models that aren't healthy (`not_healthy`). With `model_id`, the reply is that model, every version (oldest first), every validation (newest first) and `linked`: the risks that link to it, highest residual first, each with its source ("Mynt", "App: <name>" or "Product: <name>").

**`admin_list_product_risk_models({ query?, limit? })`** reads the risk models financial products declare in their definitions, across every firm. Each comes with its product (id, name, status) and its firm (none for a reference product). It is read-only.

### Audit and operations for risk models

- Every change is audited, in the obligations class: `add_risk_model`, `update_risk_model`, `validate_risk_model`, `retire_risk_model`.
- `ops_status` counts models past their next validation date (`risk_models.overdue_validations`, null on a server without them) and says so under what needs attention.
- `ops_status` also counts the models that aren't retired and aren't healthy (`risk_models.not_healthy`, with each one's name and health in `risk_models.unhealthy`), and names them under what needs attention.

## Risk in Studio

Risk shows in four places in Mynt Studio:

| Where | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| An app's **Security & risk** tab | The app's risk register, among the tab's sections |
| A product's **Risk** tab, in the product workspace at `/products/<id>` | The product's risk register |
| The platform admin's **Risk register** section (`/platform/risk-register`) | Mynt's own register, one risk area per tab. Mynt admins only |
| The platform admin's **Risk models** section (`/platform/risk-models`) | Mynt's risk models, one risk area per tab. Mynt admins only |

A register is a table of risks: title, category, the three scores **Inherent**, **Control** and **Residual** (each level in words with its number; "Not assessed" for a control nobody has assessed), owner, status in words and review-by date, highest residual first. Whoever keeps the register (`can_manage`) has a labelled **Add risk** button and a **Review risk** button on each row, each opening a sheet. Review risk also sets the control's effectiveness and, when the derived score doesn't fit, the keeper's own residual with why.

### A risk's detail

A row opens the risk's detail, by a click or its labelled **Open**: in a sheet on an app's or a product's tab, and as its own page on the platform (`/platform/risk-register/<id>`). It is one component in all three places.

The metadata card is headed "‹short id› · ‹risk area› · ‹title›" with the status in words, and holds these facts in order:

| Fact | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| Status | In words |
| Inherent | Likelihood × impact = score, with its level in words |
| Control | The control's effectiveness in words, or "Not assessed" |
| Residual | The score with its level in words; "overridden" when the keeper set it; "same as inherent" while the control isn't assessed |
| Owner | The owner, or "No owner" |
| Next review | The review date, with "overdue" in words once it has passed |
| Treatment due | The earliest due date among the open treatment tasks |
| Linked | How many items the risk links to |

Its actions are labelled buttons, each opening a sheet: **Review risk**, **Add treatment task**, **Add control**, **Link item**, **Close risk** and **Accept risk** (each needs a note), and **Copy link**. Someone who reads the register and doesn't keep it gets Copy link only.

Under the card are five tabs, each a table:

| Tab | Columns | Actions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scoring | Three tables, Impact factors, Likelihood factors and Control factors: Factor, Score, Rationale, Source, Action. Each table's caption states its formula in words, the score it explains and the factors' average | Add factor, Edit factor, Remove factor |
| Treatment | Task, Owner, Due, Status, Progress, Effectiveness, Action | Add treatment task, Update task, and Make this a control on a done task |
| Controls | Control, Kind, Last tested, Result, From task, Action | Add control, Update control, Retire control |
| Linked | Type, Item (linked where it has a page), Note, Action | Link item (a picker by type), Remove link |
| History | When, Who, What changed, Score before → after | None: it is read from the audit trail |

The routes are `GET` and `POST /api/apps/<appId>/risks/<riskId>`, `/api/products/<productId>/risks/<riskId>` and `/api/admin/risks/<riskId>`. A write must come from Studio's own origin, from a signed-in account with the route's role, and carries one action with that action's own fields. An app's or a product's route answers only for a risk on that app's or that product's register.

See [The platform admin in Studio](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/platform-admin.md#the-platform-admin-in-studio) for the two platform sections and for [Risk grading](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/platform-admin.md#platform-settings) in Platform settings.

pages.title: Vendors
pages.markdown:
This file covers the standard services vendors offer per region: service types, offerings and conformance, subscriptions, the marketplace and its standard terms, vendor onboarding, how Mynt calls a vendor, the Mynt Ramp and the wire contract. It is for vendors, for builders who subscribe to services, and for Mynt admins who define service types.

See also: [Services](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/services.md), [Roles and tools](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/roles-and-tools.md), [Agreements](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/agreements.md), [Runtime API](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/runtime-api.md), [Money rails](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/money-rails.md), [Platform administration](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/platform-admin.md).

Vendors are firms that offer standard services builders plug into their products, so that no builder has to integrate identity, verification, account data, bureau or ramp providers itself. Mynt Studio calls vendors "service providers".

A vendor's firm is a legal entity a Mynt admin adds by hand with `register_firm`. There is no self-serve discovery. To set one up:

1. A Mynt admin registers the firm (`register_firm`).
2. The admin invites the vendor's people with the `vendor` role (`invite_user`) and attaches them to the firm (`add_entity_member`). Both can be done before the person has signed in: they join the firm when they first do.
3. The vendor registers its licences (`register_license`), and an admin verifies them as for any firm.

A vendor serves its offerings in one of two ways: at its own endpoints, as this file describes, or as a **service built on Mynt**, the third kind of thing built there beside apps and financial products. A service is built, verified and hosted like an app, its endpoint is derived by Mynt, and its stage is its listing. See [Services](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/services.md).

## Service types

Like regulators, service types are defined per region. Mynt admins define them with `define_service_type`; vendors and builders read them with `list_service_types`.

### What a service type holds

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `key`, `region`, `name` | Its identity |
| `category` | One of `identity`, `kyc`, `account_data`, `analytics`, `credit_bureau`, `documents`, `esign`, `mandate`, `fraud`, `ramp`, `other` |
| `input_schema`, `output_schema` | JSON Schema: the one contract every vendor in that region implements |
| `consent_purpose` | The consent the customer must give |
| `fills` | The data dictionary fields its output fills |
| `innovator_licences` | Licence types, from the region's regulatory model, of which the subscribing firm must hold one |
| `vendor_licences` | Licence types of which the vendor must hold one |
| `moves_money` | Whether it instructs a money movement (see [Declaring what moves money](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/vendors-and-marketplace.md#declaring-what-moves-money)) |

Required inputs are data dictionary fields, because Mynt sends them from the customer's vault.

### The service types that ship

Examples ship as JSON in [`core/schemas/service-types/`](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/core/schemas/service-types). `load_service_types` loads them. An example that names a licence type your regulatory model calls something else is skipped, with the reason, until you pass `licence_map`.

The nine US service types, in `core/schemas/service-types/us`:

| Key | Service |
| --- | --- |
| `bank_account_verification` | Bank account verification |
| `credit_bureau_report` | Credit bureau report |
| `identity_verification` | Identity and SSN verification |
| `kyb_business_verification` | Business verification (state good standing) |
| `onramp_quote` | Mynt Ramp: add dollars quote |
| `onramp_transfer` | Mynt Ramp: add dollars |
| `offramp_quote` | Mynt Ramp: dollars out quote |
| `offramp_transfer` | Mynt Ramp: cash out dollars |
| `smart_contract_audit` | Smart contract audit |

The India examples, in `core/schemas/service-types/in`, ship as data only: PAN verification, CKYC search and download, Account Aggregator data fetch, bank statement analytics, credit bureau report, DigiLocker documents, eSign and e-mandate. No Indian products run today.

### What a device may be told

An optional `client_result` says what a customer's device may be told when it starts an action this service serves.

- `status` maps an output property's values to `verified`, `not_verified`, `completed`, `failed` or `pending`. Anything else is `completed`.
- `fields` lists output properties the device may see. It never lists data dictionary fields that are personal or sensitive, nor ones the service fills.
- `redirect: true` lets the device have the vendor's `redirect_url`: the provider's page, for e-sign, e-mandate and DigiLocker.

Without `client_result` the device gets a status and a reference only.

In the examples: PAN and identity verification and bank account verification give a mapped status only; bureau reports a status only; e-sign and e-mandate a mapped status and the redirect; DigiLocker the redirect.

## Offerings and conformance

### Creating an offering

`create_vendor_offering` offers a service type in a region. It names:

- a test HTTPS endpoint, and later a live one. The test endpoint may be left out of a new draft, so a vendor can [practise first](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/vendors-and-marketplace.md#practising-first-the-vendor-sandbox); `run_conformance` and listing need it (`update_vendor_offering { test_base_url }`);
- a fixed price per call, for builders to see. Billing is between vendor and builder, never through Mynt;
- service-level agreement (SLA) notes;
- the firm's licences it relies on.

An offering starts as `draft`. `list_my_offerings` lists a vendor's own.

### Conformance

Mynt tests the offering itself with `run_conformance`:

- signed requests with fixture inputs valid against the input schema, and every answer checked against the output schema;
- a badly signed request, and a correctly signed but stale one (over 300 seconds old), which must both be refused;
- timeouts and errors recorded;
- the vendor's licences checked against the service type.

A pass makes the offering `conformance_passed`. `update_vendor_offering { listed: true }` then lists it. Changing an endpoint or licences sends it back to draft.

A [service built on Mynt](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/services.md#a-new-build-and-conformance) is different: a new build goes online beside the one serving, Mynt runs the test against it itself as soon as it answers, and the offering switches to it only on a pass. The serving build stays listed and callable throughout, and the service's stage decides the listing. A service in Staging that has passed can be [tested in the sandbox by its offering id](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/services.md#testing-a-service-in-staging).

### Practising first: the vendor sandbox

A vendor that has no test endpoint yet can still see Mynt's test run. Mynt serves a practice endpoint itself for every offering (`core/src/vendor-sandbox.ts`):

```http
POST <PUBLIC_URL>/vendor-sandbox/<offering_id>
```

(`<PUBLIC_URL>/vendor-sandbox/<offering_id>/v1/<service_type_key>` is the same endpoint, in the wire contract's own shape.)

It behaves as a correct vendor of the offering's service type:

- it verifies `Mynt-Signature` with the offering's conformance signing secret, and answers `401` to a bad signature or one more than 300 seconds old (and to an offering that doesn't exist, so it never says which do);
- it checks `input` against the service type's input schema;
- it answers with a fixture `output` valid against the output schema, built from the schema itself: a property's `const`, `default`, first `examples` value or first `enum` value, else Mynt's sandbox fixture for a data dictionary field of that name, else the simplest value its type, format and pattern allow. The same schema always gives the same answer (a quote's `expires_at` is one minute ahead). If Mynt can't build a valid answer for a schema it says so (`no_sandbox_answer`) and never sends an invalid one;
- it takes bodies up to 64 KB, 30 requests a minute per offering, makes no outbound call, and keeps nothing a caller sends. Its inputs are Mynt's sandbox fixtures, never customer data.

`run_practice_conformance { offering_id }` runs **the same test cases as `run_conformance`** against that endpoint, in-process, so nothing leaves Mynt and no credential is needed (ten runs a minute per offering). It returns:

- `kind: "practice"`, `passed`, `counts_as_conformance: false`, the offering's unchanged `status`, and each case's result;
- `reference`: what Mynt sends and expects for the service type, to build an endpoint against. It has the request (`sends`: method, address, the signature rule, the input and params schemas), the answer (`expects`: the shape, the time limit and the output schema), and `transcript`: every request Mynt sent in the run and the answer it got, with what Mynt expected of each. The signing secret is never in it, and each `Mynt-Signature` is shown as `t=<seconds>,v1=<redacted>`.

On a pass it says: "Practice run passed — now point Mynt at your own test endpoint and run the real test".

A practice pass is never conformance:

- **It never moves an offering.** A practice run doesn't change an offering's status, so it never makes one `conformance_passed`, and listing still needs a real pass on the vendor's own endpoint.
- **It is recorded apart.** Practice runs are kept in their own table (`vendor_practice_runs`, `kind: "practice"`), which nothing that reads conformance reads: not listing, not the marketplace's conformance result, not `list_my_offerings`' `last_conformance`, not `ops_status` or the risk register.
- **The sandbox answers practice only.** A practice request is marked `consent.artefact_ref: "mynt_practice"`; the real test marks its requests `mynt_conformance`, which the sandbox refuses (`practice_only`). So the real test fails against the sandbox however a request reaches it.
- **The sandbox is never an offering's endpoint.** `create_vendor_offering` and `update_vendor_offering` refuse a test or live endpoint whose path is `/vendor-sandbox`, and `run_conformance` refuses again.

An admin running it for another firm's offering is audited as `admin_run_practice_conformance`.

### Suspension and admin changes

- A Mynt admin can suspend an offering with `suspend_vendor_offering`, which stops listing and calls.
- An admin's changes to another firm's offering are audited as admin actions (`admin_update_vendor_offering` and the like), naming the firm.

## Subscriptions

### Finding and subscribing

`list_vendor_offerings` shows listed offerings by region, service type or category, and whether your firm meets the licence prerequisites.

`subscribe_vendor_service` checks the prerequisites and then:

- keeps the credentials the vendor issued you (if it needs any) in your firm's key vault. The vault holds one row per key, typed `vendor_test_credential` or `vendor_live_credential`, sealed with `MYNT_VAULT_KEY` and never shown again;
- sends the test credential only to the test endpoint and the live one only to the live endpoint;
- adds the vendor's firm to your roster as a party, so the regime check and drift see it.

Bind a product's partner handoff to the subscription in its definition (see [Handoffs to a vendor's standard service](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/products.md#handoffs-to-a-vendors-standard-service)). `list_my_vendor_subscriptions` lists a firm's subscriptions.

### Test and live

- Sandbox sessions use the vendor's test endpoint.
- `set_subscription_live` turns live calls on, with the live credential if one is needed.
- Live calls go only to a listed offering, and both sides' licence prerequisites are re-checked on every call.

### Pins and drift

The subscription's state (active, offering not suspended, both sides' licences in force) is pinned with each product version that uses it. A suspension or a lapsed licence drifts those products, pausing new sales and sending `product.drifted`, until it is restored.

### Unsubscribing

`unsubscribe_vendor_service` is refused while a live product version hands off through the subscription. Otherwise it deletes the credentials and, if the vendor joined your roster for it, ends that party. Apps built on the product change nothing.

### The signing secret

The signing secret is per subscription, and Mynt generates it.

- `list_my_subscribers` says whether it has been taken.
- `reveal_subscription_secret` shows it to the vendor once.
- `rotate_subscription_secret` replaces it. The new one is shown once, and the old one stops verifying at once.

Conformance runs use the offering's own secret, shown once by `create_vendor_offering`.

A [service built on Mynt](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/services.md#the-endpoint-and-the-signing-secret) has one secret for conformance and every subscriber, handed to it only as a hosted setting and never shown. Each new build gets a new one, which takes over together with the build.

## The marketplace and standard terms

Vendor agreements are a marketplace, not a negotiation. Each offering carries the vendor's standard terms, and a subscriber accepts them by click-through.

### Standard terms

A vendor sets terms with `create_vendor_offering` or `update_vendor_offering`, as `standard_terms`:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `document_url` | A link to the terms document (https) |
| `document_sha256` | Its SHA-256, 64 lowercase hex characters |
| `summary` | A short summary |
| `pricing_summary` | The pricing in words. The vendor bills subscribers directly; Mynt never bills or holds money for it |
| `scopes` | Required. What the terms cover: one or more of the agreement scopes `technology`, `manpower` and `financial_regulatory_operations`, each once (see [Scopes](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/agreements.md#scopes)) |

- Each change, a change of scopes included, is a new `version`. The same terms set again keep their version, whatever order the scopes are named in.
- Each new version is audited as `set_vendor_terms` with its scopes.
- Terms versions set before scopes were recorded keep none. They stay as they were until the vendor sets new terms, which then name them.
- Only the vendor's own members set terms, never a Mynt admin for it.
- Listing an offering with terms is the vendor's standing acceptance of them. Who set them and when is kept.

### What a subscriber sees

`list_vendor_offerings` shows each offering's:

- `standard_terms`: version, document link and SHA-256, summary, pricing, `scopes` and `scope_labels` (empty for a version from before scopes). It is `null` when none are on file;
- last conformance result (`null` before any run);
- whether your firm meets the licence prerequisites;
- `your_subscription_id`.

### Accepting terms by click-through

Subscribing to an offering with terms is click-through:

```json
{ "offering_id": "…", "accept_terms_version": 3, "app_ids": ["…"], "products": ["…"], "test_credential": "…" }
```

`subscribe_vendor_service` must name:

- `accept_terms_version`: the current version. An older one is refused, naming the current;
- `app_ids`: the apps it is for. The caller must be an owner or admin of each app's workspace;
- optionally `products`: the apps' products it is used for.

In one transaction Mynt records the subscription and, per app, an app agreement of kind `vendor` with the vendor's firm, already `signed`:

- by the vendor through its listing. Its signer and time are the terms' setter and time;
- by the subscriber through the click;
- with the version, document link, SHA-256, summary, pricing and scopes accepted. The scopes are the accepted version's own: an agreement on a version from before scopes records none ("Not set"), never invented ones.

Each is audited as `accept_vendor_terms`, in the obligations class, with the app's id, and the vendor is told (`app_agreement.signed`).

- A firm already subscribed names more apps the same way, to accept the current version for them too.
- A later version doesn't change agreements already made.
- Prerequisites are checked as for any subscription.

### Ending an agreement

The agreement and the subscription end together.

- `unsubscribe_vendor_service({ subscription_id, reason? })` ends every agreement accepted with it, audited as `terminate_app_agreement`, and the vendor is told.
- `terminate_app_agreement` by either side on the last open agreement of a subscription ends the subscription too.
- Both are refused while a live product version hands off through the subscription.

### What vendors and older subscribers see

- Vendors see their subscribers with the version and scopes each accepted, per app, in `list_my_subscribers`' `terms_accepted`, and the agreements in `list_app_agreements` without `app_id`.
- Subscriptions made before an offering had terms stay as they were. `list_app_agreements`' `vendor_contracts` flags them `no_standard_terms: true`, and `terms_accepted` is `null` elsewhere.
- A negotiated `vendor` agreement (`propose_app_agreement`) is still possible beside a click-through one.

### Appearing in the marketplace

To appear in the marketplace:

1. A Mynt admin adds the vendor's firm (`register_firm`) and its people with the `vendor` role.
2. The vendor creates an offering of a service type in its region.
3. The offering passes Mynt's conformance test.
4. The vendor lists it (`update_vendor_offering { listed: true }`).
5. The vendor sets its standard terms.

In Mynt Studio, the Marketplace page (`/marketplace`, for builders) lists those offerings with a Subscribe sheet. An offering's Standard terms tab and the Subscribe sheet show the scope being accepted ("You accept <vendor>'s standard terms v<n> — Scope: …"). The vendor's Set standard terms sheet has the required Scope checkboxes.

## Onboarding a vendor

`get_vendor_onboarding` shows where a vendor's onboarding stands as one ordered checklist: for the firm, then for each of its offerings. It only reads. Each step is done with the tools it names, which decide as before.

| Caller | Reads |
| --- | --- |
| A vendor's own member | Their firm's: no arguments, or their own `entity_id` |
| A Mynt admin | Any firm's (`entity_id`, or `offering_id` alone), and every vendor firm's progress (`all_firms: true`: firms with a member holding the vendor role, someone invited with it who hasn't signed in yet, or an offering) |

### Steps and statuses

Each step has a `key`, a `title`, a `status`, a `detail` in plain words, the `tool` that does it, `by` (`vendor`, `admin` or `subscriber`) and `facts`.

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `done` | The step is complete |
| `next` | The first thing the vendor can do now. One per checklist |
| `not_started` | The vendor's to do, after the next one |
| `blocked` | Waiting on Mynt, or on an earlier step. The detail says which, for example "Waiting for Mynt to verify your licence rbi_pa (PA-1)" |

### The checklist

| Step | Done when | Otherwise |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `firm_registered` (firm) | The firm is on Mynt and `active` | Blocked on an admin (`register_firm`, `set_entity_status`). Every step after it waits too |
| `vendor_members` (firm) | Someone at the firm has the vendor role (`facts.members`) | Blocked on an admin (`invite_user`, `add_entity_member`). Once people are invited, it waits for them to sign in (`facts.invited`) |
| `first_service` (firm) | The firm has an offering | Next: `create_vendor_offering`. Blocked while nobody at the firm has the vendor role |
| `service_created` (offering) | Always, with its service type and region | |
| `licence` (offering, only when the service type needs a vendor licence) | A verified, in-force licence of one of the types is named on the offering | Register one (`register_license`). Blocked while Mynt verifies it (`review_license`) or has suspended it. Register again if rejected or lapsed. Name it on the offering (`update_vendor_offering { licence_ids }`) |
| `practice` (offering, informational) | The latest `run_practice_conformance` passed (`facts.last_run`, `facts.counts_as_conformance: false`). The detail says to point Mynt at the vendor's own endpoint and run the real test | Not started: optional, never counted, and never the `conformance` step (see [Practising first](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/vendors-and-marketplace.md#practising-first-the-vendor-sandbox)) |
| `conformance` (offering) | The latest `run_conformance` passed and the offering is `conformance_passed` or `listed` (`facts.last_run`: when, who, failures; `facts.test_endpoint`: whether the offering has its own) | Run it, or run it again after a failure (named in the detail) or a change of endpoint or licences. With no test endpoint yet, give one first (`update_vendor_offering { test_base_url }`). Blocked while the licence waits on Mynt |
| `terms` (offering) | Standard terms naming their scopes are on file (`facts.terms_version`, `facts.scopes`) | Set them, with their scopes (`update_vendor_offering { standard_terms }`). App teams can't subscribe from the Marketplace without them |
| `listed` (offering) | Listed | List it once it passed (`update_vendor_offering { listed: true }`) |
| `first_subscriber` (offering, informational) | A firm subscribes (`facts.subscribers`) | Not started: it is the subscribers' choice, and never counted |

An offering can be listed before it has standard terms. Both steps then say the same thing: `listed` is done, "without standard terms: app teams can't subscribe until you set them", and `terms` is the next step.

Terms from before scopes were recorded stand, and subscribers can still accept them, but the `terms` step stays to do until new terms name their scopes.

A suspended offering's steps wait on Mynt (`suspend_vendor_offering`). Terms already set stay done.

### Progress and history

`progress`, per offering and for the firm, counts the steps done out of those counted, names the `next` one (the vendor's own first, else what waits on Mynt) and says whether it is `complete`.

With `offering_id`, `history` adds:

- that offering's conformance runs, newest first, up to 20;
- its practice runs (`practice_runs`), apart from them, newest first, up to 20;
- every version of its standard terms Mynt knows: the current one in full, and earlier ones from the audit log (version, SHA-256, scopes, when, by whom) and from the agreements that accepted them, with how many did.

A figure Mynt doesn't keep (an earlier version's summary nobody accepted, a firm not yet registered) is `null`, never 0.

### My services in Studio

Mynt Studio shows the checklist to vendors as My services (`/vendor`, in the sidebar only for accounts with the vendor role):

- the checklist on top, each step's status in words, with a labelled button where Studio can do it: Create service, Run practice test, Run conformance, Set standard terms, List service. The practice run is a line "for information";
- the firm's services in a table;
- each service's details: Conformance runs, Practice runs, Terms versions, Subscribers;
- Run practice test, beside Run conformance on a service, opens a sheet with each case's result, what Mynt sends and expects, and the run's transcript (Download transcript saves it as JSON). Create service takes a service with no test endpoint yet, to practise on.

A service built on Mynt has its own workspace at `/services/<id>` (see [Mynt Studio](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/studio.md)); My services lists it beside the offerings served elsewhere.

The platform admin's Vendors section has a Vendor firms tab with each firm's onboarding progress (see [The platform admin in Studio](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/platform-admin.md#the-platform-admin-in-studio)).

## Calling a vendor's service

### Client actions served by the vendor

When a product's partner handoff is bound to a subscription, its client action (`POST /v1/client/actions/<handoff>`) is served by Mynt calling the vendor, instead of handing off to the product builder's URL. That holds whatever the service: identity, bureau, e-sign, e-mandate, KYC.

The developer contract marks the action `served_by: { kind: "vendor_service", service_type, client_result }`. It carries no subscription, vendor, URL or secret.

What the device needs:

- a client session with a `customer_ref`;
- the service's consent (`409 consent_required` otherwise);
- its required inputs in the vault (`409 data_required` otherwise). Only the service type's declared inputs are sent.

Which endpoint is called:

- Sandbox sessions call the test endpoint with the test credential.
- Live sessions call the live endpoint with the live credential, once the product's builder turned the subscription live (`503 vendor_unavailable` before), and only for a listed offering with both sides' licences in force.

An answer that breaks the output schema is `502 vendor_error`, and nothing is kept.

### What happens to a good answer

A good answer is:

- kept by Mynt, sealed, for the session, with evidence `action_completed` (or `action_failed`) of the action (status only), and the fields the service fills saved to the customer's vault;
- sent in full to the product builder's firm webhooks (see [Firm webhooks](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/vendors-and-marketplace.md#firm-webhooks)) as `vendor_action.completed`. `vendor_action.failed` carries no result;
- answered to the device with only `{ reference, action, status, sandbox }` plus what the service type's `client_result` allows.

`GET /v1/client/action_runs/<reference>` reads the device's answer back, for the same app and customer.

Handoffs not bound to a vendor keep the hand-off to the product builder's own flow.

### Asynchronous services

Asynchronous services (e-sign, e-mandate, DigiLocker) may answer the call with:

```json
{ "request_id": "…", "status": "pending", "redirect_url": "https://…" }
```

The device gets `status: "pending"` and, when the service type allows it, the `redirect_url`.

The vendor then sends the final answer to `POST /v1/vendor/callback/<subscription_id>`, signed exactly like Mynt's requests: `Mynt-Signature` with the subscription's signing secret, at most 300 seconds old (`401` otherwise). Its body is:

```json
{ "request_id": "<Mynt's>", "status": "ok", "output": {} }
```

`status` is `ok` or `error`.

- An output that breaks the schema is refused (`400 invalid_output`) and changes nothing. A good one completes the action as above.
- A repeated `request_id` is answered with `duplicate: true` and applied once.
- A valid answer whose own status maps to `pending` (the customer hasn't finished yet) also leaves the action open for the callback.
- One that maps to `failed` ends the action as failed (`action_failed`, and `vendor_action.failed` with the result).
- When an asynchronous action ends, the app's own webhooks get `handoff.completed` or `handoff.failed` with only the product, `reference`, `action` and `status`.

### The customer stays in control

- A callback that arrives after the customer withdrew the service's consent ends the action as withdrawn. Nothing of the answer is kept, and the product's builder gets `vendor_action.failed` with `error_code: "consent_withdrawn"` and no result.
- `DELETE /v1/client/fields` also erases the vendor results kept for the customer and any still queued for the product's builder, and stops their open actions.
- Actions that never finish expire (`error_code: "expired"`): a call cut short after 5 minutes, a pending one after `VENDOR_PENDING_EXPIRY_HOURS` (default 24).
- Callbacks are rate limited per caller address before the signature is checked, and per subscription only once it is.
- Sandbox results are sealed with a key derived from `MYNT_VAULT_KEY`, so a queued delivery survives a restart.

### Params and quotes

Two optional parts of a service type let a device ask for something specific and act on a price.

**Params.** `params_schema` (with `params_fixture` for conformance) declares what the device sends with each call, as `params` in `POST /v1/client/actions/<handoff>`: an amount, a currency, an asset.

- It must be an object of plain scalar properties with `additionalProperties: false`.
- It must never hold a data dictionary field that is customer data. That comes from the vault, as `input`.
- Mynt checks the params against it before calling (`400 invalid_params`). An action that takes none refuses them (`400 params_not_accepted`).

**Quotes.** `quote: true` makes the service a quote. Its output must require `quote_id` and `expires_at`, in the future and at most an hour ahead (`502 vendor_error` otherwise). The device gets `expires_at` and whatever `client_result` allows, never `quote_id`.

A service type with `accepts: "<quote key>"` (same region and category) accepts a quote.

- The device starts it with `quote: "<the quote's reference>"`, and Mynt sends the vendor `quote: { quote_id }`.
- That works only for a quote of the same app, customer, product and environment, from the same vendor, unexpired and not accepted before (`404 quote_not_found`, `409 quote_expired`, `409 quote_used`).
- Claiming a quote is atomic, so two accepts of one quote can't both go through.
- A call that fails or is refused releases the quote for another try, so vendors must treat a repeated `quote_id` as the same order.

In the developer contract, such an action's `served_by` carries `params_schema`, `quote: true`, or `accepts_quote_from: "<the quoting action>"`. The SDKs' `startAction` takes `params` and `quote`.

### Declaring what moves money

Every service type sets `moves_money`. It is `true` when the service instructs a money movement, which sends it through approved money rails (see [Money rails](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/money-rails.md)).

- `ops_status` reports a stored type whose name says it moves money but which is declared `false`.
- A service type can't fill `residence_state`. A partner-verified state comes as `residential_state` in an identity service's output (see [Partner requirements](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/money-rails.md#partner-requirements)).
- A ramp offering's `test_base_url` and `live_base_url` must be different endpoints, however they are written.

## The Mynt Ramp

All dollars in and out of digital-asset liquidity go through one ramp.

- Its service types have the category `ramp`.
- Only the firm a Mynt admin designates with `set_mynt_ramp` (audited) may offer or list them. That firm is the ramp partner, which holds funds in transit and transmits money under its own licences. Mynt never holds funds or keys.
- Mynt calls only that firm's ramp offerings, in sandbox and live. Re-designating the ramp stops calls to the old firm's at once.
- Builders subscribe to the ramp and bind handoffs to it like any vendor service.

### The four ramp service types

The shipped US types come in two pairs, each with its own consent purpose.

| Pair | Quote | Accepted by | Consent |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Add dollars | `onramp_quote` | `onramp_transfer` | `fiat_onramp` |
| Cash out | `offramp_quote` | `offramp_transfer` | `fiat_offramp` |

A quote takes params `direction` (`in` or `out`) and `amount_usd`, and the customer's name and bank account from the vault. The device is shown `amount_usd`, `fee_usd`, `total_usd` (in: added to the balance; out: taken from it), `currency` (`USD`), `estimated_arrival` and `expires_at`.

A transfer usually answers pending until the bank transfer settles: `submitted`, then `settled`, `failed` or `returned`. When the customer pushes the payment, an add-dollars transfer also shows the US bank account to pay: `pay_to_bank_name`, `pay_to_account_number`, `pay_to_routing_number` and `pay_to_reference`.

The settlement leg (`settlement_asset` USDC, `settlement_network` solana, `settlement_amount`, `settlement_ref`, `settlement_tx`) is in the output, sealed to the product's builder, and never reaches a device.

All four name the licence type `fincen_msb`. Map it to yours with `licence_map`.

### Dollars only for customers

A builder's customers never see or touch crypto. Every customer-facing value is a US dollar amount, a fee, a total, a status, an arrival time or a reference.

Mynt enforces it in code (`core/src/dollars-only.ts`):

- `define_service_type` refuses a `client_result` field or a `params_schema` property whose name carries a crypto concept (asset, chain, network, wallet, address, tx, hash, token, coin, memo, a token symbol or chain name), or whose enum, const or default is a token symbol or chain name.
- It refuses a ramp currency field that isn't `USD`.
- It refuses a service type name that names a crypto concept, because the name reaches devices in error messages.
- Publishing refuses a binding to a service type stored before the rule.
- The developer contract drops such fields.
- The device's outcome drops any field, or any value that looks like a token, a chain, an address or a transaction hash, whatever the service type says.

Keep the settlement asset in the output, where it goes sealed to the product's builder.

### How the ramp partner plugs in

There are two ways. Either way, Mynt's quote and accept, conformance, callbacks and the dollars-only rule are the same.

1. **The wire contract.** The partner serves Mynt's vendor wire contract at its offerings' base URLs (see [The wire contract](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/vendors-and-marketplace.md#the-wire-contract)).
2. **An adapter in front of its own API** (`core/src/ramp-adapters/`). The ramp firm, or a Mynt admin, runs `set_ramp_adapter { offering_id, adapter, config?, test_credential?, live_credential? }` on each ramp offering.

With an adapter:

- The offering's base URLs are the partner's API.
- The credentials go sealed into the ramp firm's key vault (key types `ramp_partner_test_credential` and `ramp_partner_live_credential`). They are never shown, logged or put in the audit log.
- Mynt answers its own signed requests in-process. The adapter is a small typed interface (`probe`, `price`, `transfer`, `status`, `webhook`) that translates each request to the partner's API, and the partner's states and webhooks back to Mynt's.
- Partner webhooks go to `<PUBLIC_URL>/v1/ramp-adapters/<offering_id>/webhook/<test|live>`, verified with the partner's own scheme. Transfers whose webhook hasn't come are read back every minute.
- Conformance probes the partner with the credential and moves no money.
- Test and live stay apart. A URL or key that looks like the partner's other environment (by its documented hosts and key prefixes) is refused, and conformance probes both credentials when both are set.

### Linking a customer to the partner

The customer starts the link, from their own session and after giving the ramp's consent there.

1. `POST /v1/client/ramp_links { product_id }` answers a `link_reference`.
2. The ramp firm gets `ramp_link.requested` with only that reference, never the builder's customer reference.
3. Once the partner has onboarded the customer, the ramp firm completes it with `link_ramp_partner_customer { link_reference, partner_customer_id, partner_payout_account_id? }`.

Mynt reads the partner's identity for that customer through the adapter and links only if:

- the name matches what the customer gave Mynt, compared in any script after Unicode normalisation (an empty name never matches);
- in live, the date of birth matches too (in test, when both have one);
- the payout account is that partner customer's own;
- the partner customer is linked to one Mynt customer only.

Otherwise the request is refused.

A session may ask five times an hour, and a customer ten times a day. A request expires after seven days (`RAMP_LINK_EXPIRY_HOURS`). Transfers and payouts use only a verified link, filed under a pseudonymous key.

### A transfer's life

Statuses only move forward: `submitted`, then `settled`, `failed` or `returned`. An earlier state arriving late is ignored, and each partner event is applied once, by its event id.

**Waiting for payment.** An add-dollars transfer waits for the customer's payment for business days, not the 24 hours other vendor actions get (`pending_business_days`, default 7, or `RAMP_ADAPTER_PENDING_BUSINESS_DAYS`).

- Past that, Mynt voids it at the partner when the partner can, and the run fails.
- `pay_to_status` is `active` while the account can be paid into. It becomes `void` when the partner confirmed the void and `unknown` when it couldn't. Either way the app tells the customer not to pay into that account.
- A transfer the partner won't void, because its money is already moving, keeps waiting, up to 30 business days.

**Late settlement.** Money that settles after the run ended is never dropped. It is kept sealed on the run and the product's builder gets `vendor_action.late_settlement` to handle by hand.

**Reversal.** A settled transfer the bank later sends back (returned or refunded) is the one change after the end. The run becomes `reversed`, the device sees `failed` with `reversed: true`, the product's builder gets `vendor_action.reversed` (sealed details) and the app a data-free `handoff.reversed`.

**Amounts.** A transfer's amounts are what the partner reports, never an assumed 1:1. `total_usd` means what it means in that leg's quote: in, added to the balance; out, what the customer is charged, amount plus fees. A cash-out's `paid_out_usd` is what reached the bank.

A run ends before its transfer's record moves on, so a failure part-way is finished by the partner's retry or the poller, never lost.

### The Bridge adapter

The Bridge adapter (`adapter: "bridge"`, [apidocs.bridge.xyz](https://apidocs.bridge.xyz)) is the reference adapter.

| Topic | How |
| --- | --- |
| Base URLs | `https://api.sandbox.bridge.xyz` and `https://api.bridge.xyz` |
| Authentication | `Api-Key` |
| Idempotency | `Idempotency-Key` on every transfer, one per quote, so a retry never moves money twice |
| Quotes | Bridge has no quote that locks a price, so Mynt issues it. The fee (`fee_percent`, default 0.5, at least `fee_min_usd`, default 0.50) is charged as Bridge's `developer_fee`, and Mynt sets the validity (`quote_seconds`, default 60) |
| Add dollars | `POST /v0/transfers` from `ach_push` USD to USDC on `solana` at the ramp's `settlement_address`. The customer is shown Bridge's deposit account and deposit message |
| Cash out | USDC on `solana` from that address to `ach` USD at the customer's payout account |
| Webhooks | Verified with the endpoint's public key (`test_webhook_public_key`, `live_webhook_public_key`): `X-Webhook-Signature`, at most 10 minutes old |
| Voiding | An unpaid add-dollars transfer is voided with `DELETE /v0/transfers/{id}`. Bridge cancels only while `awaiting_funds` |
| Identity | A customer's identity is read with `GET /v0/customers/{id}` |
| Limits | Each transfer is between `min_usd` (default 1.00) and `max_usd` (default 10000.00) |

Bridge's states map to Mynt's:

| Bridge | Mynt |
| --- | --- |
| `payment_processed` | `settled` |
| `returned`, `refund_in_flight`, `refunded` | `returned` |
| `undeliverable`, `canceled`, `refund_failed` | `failed` |
| anything else | `submitted` |

Cash-out through Bridge isn't built yet. It needs the USDC leg from the ramp's settlement address into Bridge, so `offramp_quote` and `offramp_transfer` are refused on a Bridge offering, always in live. `test_offramp: "true"` lets them run in the test environment only.

### The Mynt Ramp sandbox

Mynt serves a test ramp itself at `<PUBLIC_URL>/ramp-sandbox` (`core/src/ramp-sandbox.ts`), so apps can be built and tested on both ramps before the partner's live endpoint exists.

- The ramp firm sets its offerings' `test_base_url` to it (`set_mynt_ramp` shows the address) and its `live_base_url` to the partner's.
- It speaks the same wire contract, answers only requests Mynt signed for a ramp offering pointed at it, refuses live requests, and never moves money.
- Prices are in dollars with a 0.5% fee (at least $0.50). The settlement leg is 1:1.
- Transfers settle a few seconds later (`RAMP_SANDBOX_SETTLE_MS`, default 3000) through Mynt's own signed callback.
- An amount ending in `.13` comes back `returned` and one ending in `.66` `failed`.

## Usage

Mynt counts calls per subscription and day: successes and errors, never customer data.

- Vendors see them in `list_my_subscribers`.
- Builders see them in `list_my_vendor_subscriptions`.
- `ops_status` lists failed conformance runs and subscriptions whose calls mostly fail.

## Firm webhooks

A firm gets events at its own webhooks about what Mynt did for it. They are separate from an app's webhooks (see [Webhooks](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/runtime-api.md#webhooks)), and customers never see them.

| Tool | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `create_firm_webhook` | Registers an https URL for the firm, with the events it wants |
| `list_firm_webhooks` | Lists the firm's webhooks with their recent deliveries (status and response code only) |
| `delete_firm_webhook` | Removes one and drops its delivery history |

Builders and licence providers hold these tools.

### How firm events are delivered

- Each is signed with `Mynt-Signature` like an app's webhooks and retried the same way.
- A result is queued sealed and opened only to send.
- `vendor_action.completed` carries `data.result`, the product, action, app, `customer_ref`, `reference` and `sandbox`.
- Firm webhook URLs pass the same address checks as app webhook URLs (see [Webhook addresses](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/runtime-api.md#webhook-addresses)).

### Firm events

| Events | About |
| --- | --- |
| `vendor_action.completed`, `vendor_action.failed` | A client action that a product's bound vendor service answered, or that failed |
| `vendor_action.reversed` | A completed ramp transfer the partner later reversed |
| `vendor_action.late_settlement` | A transfer the partner settled after Mynt had ended the run, to handle by hand |
| `ramp_link.requested` | To the Mynt Ramp firm: a customer asked to be linked to the ramp partner |
| `program.deployed`, `program.upgraded`, `program.event` | The firm's Solana programs, deployed or upgraded by Mynt, and each Anchor event they emit |
| `program.upgrade_scheduled`, `program.upgrade_cancelled` | A mainnet upgrade passed the mainnet program gate and is announced before its timelock ends, or was cancelled or rejected |
| `program.review_flagged` | A new vulnerability database version refuses a deployed mainnet program. It keeps running; its upgrades wait for a Mynt admin's review |
| `covenant.breached`, `covenant.cleared` | To a licence provider: one of its rules on a sponsored product tripped or passed again |
| `partner_ledger.endpoint_change_pending`, `partner_ledger.endpoints_confirmed`, `partner_ledger.source_changed`, `partner_ledger.key_changed`, `partner_ledger.approval_requested`, `partner_ledger.conformance_expiring` | Changes to a licence provider's ledger connection (see [Partner kit](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/licence-providers.md#partner-kit)) |
| `confidential.release_announced` | A new release of the confidential service was announced (see [Confidential computing](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/confidential-computing.md)) |
| `firm.member_added`, `firm.member_pending`, `firm.member_standing_lost`, `firm.member_removed`, `firm.recovery_pending` | Changes to who belongs to the firm and who has licence-provider standing there |
| `app_agreement.proposed`, `app_agreement.signed`, `app_agreement.terminated`, `app_agreement.answered` | An app agreement proposed to the firm, signed, ended, or accepted or declined by the app's side |
| `agreement_audit.opened`, `agreement_audit.submitted`, `agreement_audit.closed` | An oversight audit under an app agreement opened, answered by the app's side, or closed. Told to both parties' firms |
| `agreement_sla.breached` | A service level under an app agreement was missed in a period. Told to both parties' firms |

## The wire contract

Mynt calls the vendor with:

```http
POST <base_url>/v1/<service_type_key>
Content-Type: application/json
Mynt-Signature: t=<unix seconds>,v1=<hex HMAC-SHA256 of "<t>.<raw body>">
Authorization: Bearer <the subscriber's credential>
```

The `Authorization` header is sent only when the offering requires a credential.

The body is:

```json
{
  "request_id": "…",
  "environment": "test",
  "input": {},
  "params": {},
  "quote": { "quote_id": "…" },
  "consent": {
    "purpose": "<the service type's consent_purpose>",
    "artefact_ref": "<Mynt's consent evidence id>",
    "given_at": "<ISO 8601>"
  }
}
```

- `environment` is `test` or `live`.
- `input` is valid against the service type's `input_schema`.
- `params` is sent only for a service type with a `params_schema`.
- `quote` is sent only for a service type that accepts a quote. In conformance runs its `quote_id` is `mynt_conformance`, as is `consent.artefact_ref`; in a practice run against [Mynt's sandbox](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/vendors-and-marketplace.md#practising-first-the-vendor-sandbox) both are `mynt_practice`.

Mynt expects `200` with:

```json
{
  "request_id": "<the same>",
  "status": "ok",
  "output": {},
  "error": null
}
```

- `status` is `ok` or `error`.
- `output` is valid against the service type's `output_schema`.
- `error` is `{ "code": "…", "message": "…" }` or `null`.

A vendor must answer `401` to anything whose signature doesn't verify or whose timestamp is more than 300 seconds old. It must treat a repeated `request_id` as a replay and answer it once.

The signing secret is the subscription's (see [The signing secret](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/vendors-and-marketplace.md#the-signing-secret)).

## Outbound safety

These rules apply to every call Mynt makes to a vendor.

- HTTPS on port 443 only.
- The host is resolved and refused if any address is private, loopback, link-local (including cloud metadata addresses), carrier-grade NAT or otherwise reserved. That includes site-local addresses and IPv6 forms that embed an IPv4 address: IPv4-mapped and IPv4-compatible, NAT64 and 6to4.
- Mynt connects to the address it checked.
- Redirects aren't followed.
- Each call has 10 seconds.
- Responses are capped at 256 KiB.
- Credentials and customer data never reach logs or responses.

pages.title: Services
pages.markdown:
This file covers services: the third kind of thing built on Mynt, beside apps and financial products. It is for builders who hold the vendor role and want to build a service on Mynt and list it in the Marketplace, and for Mynt admins who define service types.

See also: [Vendors and the marketplace](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/vendors-and-marketplace.md), [Apps and builds](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/apps-and-builds.md), [Mynt Studio](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/studio.md), [Roles and tools](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/roles-and-tools.md), [Platform administration](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/platform-admin.md).

## The three kinds

| Kind | What it is | Who uses it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| App | An app for customers, built on financial products | Customers |
| Financial product | A regulated product composed from primitives | Apps |
| Service | A service other builders plug into their products, listed in the Marketplace | Builders |

A service answers one of Mynt's standard service types (identity verification, a bureau report, a score) in one region. A vendor can still serve a service type from its own endpoint, as before (see [Offerings and conformance](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/vendors-and-marketplace.md#offerings-and-conformance)). A service is the same offering built, verified and hosted on Mynt.

## How a service is stored

A service is an app record of kind `service` (`apps.kind`, `app` by default), with exactly one vendor offering made with it (`vendor_offerings.app_id`, one per service).

- Builds, hosting, stages and workspaces reuse it by its id. `start_build`, `deploy_app`, `undeploy_app`, `get_promotion_checks`, `promote_app` and `demote_app` take a service's id as `app_id`.
- It belongs to a workspace, and to the firm of the person who created it.
- It has one service type and one region, no products, and is never published as an app experience.
- `list_my_apps` returns it with `kind: "service"`. `list_my_services` returns services only.

## Creating a service

`create_service` takes a name, a description, a service type and a region, and optionally a workspace, a price per call, service-level notes and the firm's licences it relies on.

It needs:

- the vendor role. A Mynt admin grants it; builders do not get it by themselves;
- a firm. The service is offered by the caller's firm;
- to be an owner or admin of the workspace it goes in.

Service types stay admin-defined (`list_service_types`). The Mynt Ramp's service types are not built as services.

The answer is the service as `get_service` returns it, with what to do next. The signing secret is never in it.

### Asking for a service type

When no service type fits, `request_service_type` asks Mynt's admins for one:

```json
{
  "name": "Income verification",
  "what_it_does": "Confirms a customer's stated income against payroll data.",
  "example_input": { "full_name": "Asha Verma" },
  "example_output": { "verified": true }
}
```

- `region` is optional (`US` by default). Each example is one JSON object under 8 KB. A person may have ten requests waiting.
- `list_service_type_requests` shows each request's status: waiting for Mynt, defined (with the service type's key) or declined (with the reason). Builders and vendors see their own and their firm's; admins see everyone's.
- An admin defines the service type from the request with `define_service_type { service_type, from_request }`, or declines it with `decline_service_type_request { request_id, reason }`.
- Each step is audited (`request_service_type`, `define_service_type` with the request's id, `decline_service_type_request`).

## The contract a build reads

`get_service_type_contract { key, region }` returns everything an endpoint for a service type implements, as one JSON document:

- the input, params and output JSON Schemas;
- the signature rule;
- the request and response shapes;
- fixture requests valid against the input schema, and an example output;
- the path a service answers at.

Nothing in it is secret. A build reads the same document three ways:

| Where | How |
| --- | --- |
| The MCP tool | `get_service_type_contract` |
| The runtime API | `GET /v1/service_types/<key>/contract?region=<region>`, with the build's sandbox key |
| The build's job | `job/service-contracts/<key>.json`, named in `job/build.json` as `service.contract` |

## What the coding agents build

A build for a service starts from `core/workspaces/coding-build/templates/mynt-service/`:

```sh
python3 scripts/scaffold_app.py <dest> --service <contract.json>
```

It is one Compose project with two parts.

- **`api/`** serves `POST /mynt/services/<service type key>`. `vendor-service.ts` verifies `Mynt-Signature`, checks the input against the contract's input schema, calls `handleService`, checks the output against the output schema and answers. `handle-service.ts` holds the one function the builder writes: `handleService(input) → output`.
- **`web/`** is a status page. A service has no customer screens, no SDK and no mobile part.

The template ships a unit test for the signature and the schemas (`npm test`). CI scaffolds a service from the contract of a shipped service type, runs those tests, then starts the service and runs Mynt's own conformance cases against it.

The app starter (`templates/mynt-app/`) is unchanged: an app never serves a service type.

## The endpoint and the signing secret

**The endpoint is derived, never typed.** It is the service's hosted address plus `/mynt/services/<service type key>`. Mynt sets it each time the service is put online. `update_vendor_offering` refuses `test_base_url`, `live_base_url` and `requires_credential` on a service's offering.

**The signature is the only authentication.**

- Mynt signs each request with `Mynt-Signature: t=<unix seconds>,v1=<hex HMAC-SHA256 of "<t>.<raw body>">`.
- The service answers `401` to a signature that doesn't verify or a timestamp more than 300 seconds from now, and compares in constant time.
- Mynt's conformance and live calls go straight to the hosted address. They carry no credential and no app key.
- The app key Mynt's hosting adds at its edge is added only to a hosted project's own calls out to Mynt's address. It is never on a call from Mynt to a service, and the endpoint must never ask for one.

**The signing secret reaches the service only as a hosted setting.**

- The build that serves has one signing secret, sealed with `MYNT_VAULT_KEY`.
- `deploy_app` hands it to the service as `MYNT_VENDOR_SIGNING_SECRET`, in the deploy job's environment, never in the job's text. It is scrubbed from a failed deploy's output.
- It is never shown: not by `create_service`, `get_service`, `list_my_offerings`, nor to the browser. It is never in the repository, and never in a run's transcript.
- Every subscriber's calls are signed with it. `reveal_subscription_secret` and `rotate_subscription_secret` refuse a service's subscriptions and say why.
- A new build that goes online beside the serving one gets a new secret of its own (see [A new build and conformance](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/services.md#a-new-build-and-conformance)).

Mynt's [outbound safety](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/vendors-and-marketplace.md#outbound-safety) rules apply to a service as to any vendor: HTTPS on port 443, and never a private, loopback or reserved address. A hosted address is the hosting provider's, not Mynt's own.

### Hosting a service needs direct hosting

A service is hosted under direct hosting only (see [Direct hosting on Freestyle](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/apps-and-builds.md#direct-hosting-on-freestyle)). On a Mynt that hosts through its gateway, `create_service` and `deploy_app` for a service refuse and say why. Nothing is half-created or half-deployed.

Gateway mode cannot host a service, for four reasons in how it works:

- A service is a Compose project, and gateway mode runs single-container apps only.
- The VM's agent is a script fixed when the VM first booted. It starts each app with its Mynt key and Mynt's address and nothing else, so there is no way to hand over the signing secret.
- Mynt never learns that a build is running there, so it cannot test a build the moment it answers.
- It has one VM per workspace and one container per app, so a new build cannot go online beside the one serving.

## Stages

A service moves through the same stages as an app, in the same sidebar folders.

| Stage | Means |
| --- | --- |
| Idea | A draft. Its offering exists and is not listed |
| Staging | Built and online. Mynt runs its conformance test; practice runs are for information. Once a build has passed, it is open to sandbox testing by its offering id |
| Production | Listed in the Marketplace, and live-subscribable |

Production is the listing. `promote_app` to production lists the offering, and `demote_app` back to staging unlists it. `update_vendor_offering { listed }` is refused on a service's offering.

### Testing a service in Staging

A service in Staging whose build has passed Mynt's conformance test is **in testing**: builders can subscribe to it and call it in the sandbox, before it is listed.

- **By its offering id only.** It is never in the Marketplace list. Its builder gives the offering id to whoever should test it (`get_service` returns it as `testing.offering_id`, and the Studio shows it). `list_vendor_offerings { offering_id }` shows that one offering, marked `availability: "in_testing"` and `sandbox_only: true`.
- **Subscribing.** `subscribe_vendor_service { offering_id }`, as for a listed offering: the same licence prerequisites, and the vendor's standard terms accepted by version when it has any on file.
- **Sandbox only.** Sandbox sessions call it. Live sessions never do: `set_subscription_live` refuses and says why, and a live call is refused whatever the subscription says.
- **Promotion carries subscribers over.** Moving the service to Production lists it. The same subscriptions go on working in the sandbox and can then be turned live with `set_subscription_live`.
- **Moving back.** `demote_app` to Staging stops live calls and takes it off the list. Its subscriptions stay, sandbox only again.

`list_my_vendor_subscriptions` shows each subscription's `availability` (`listed` or `in_testing`, with the words "In testing: sandbox only until its builder moves it to Production").

### Promotion checks

`get_promotion_checks` computes them from Mynt's own records. Moving to staging uses the same three checks as an app (the build verified, its audit, and that it runs).

Moving to production uses a service's own checks, in this order:

| Check | Passes when |
| --- | --- |
| Conformance passed on the build that is online | Mynt's latest conformance run passed against the build Mynt's hosting runs |
| Standard terms set, with their scope | The offering has standard terms that name what they cover |
| Licence verified by Mynt | A verified licence in force is named on the offering, or the service type needs none |
| Latest build verified by Mynt | A build passed Mynt's verification in a clean sandbox |
| Independent audit passed | The build's independent audit found no critical or high issue. A build with no audit warns |
| No open blocking audit findings | The audit left no critical or high finding open |
| Healthy on Mynt's hosting | The verified build runs on Mynt's hosting |

A service has no checks for target states, licence coverage by product, sponsor program agreements, webhooks or admin sign-off.

## A new build and conformance

Every build that goes online is tested before it serves anyone, and subscribers never wait for that.

**Who puts a build online.** Only an owner or admin of the service's workspace, at the firm that offers it. A build put online is handed a signing secret and, once it passes, receives subscribers' requests, so being a member of the workspace is not enough. The same people take it offline (`undeploy_app`), restart it (`restart_app`) and run commands in it (`app_run`). Every member reads its status and logs.

### When a build is serving

While a build serves subscribers (the offering is `conformance_passed` or `listed`), a new build never replaces it directly.

1. `deploy_app` puts the new build online **beside** the serving one: a second copy, on a VM and at an address of its own. The offering keeps its endpoint, its secret, its status and its place in the Marketplace. `get_service` shows the new build as `new_build`.
2. When the new copy answers, Mynt runs its conformance test against it, with nobody asking.
3. **A pass switches.** The offering's endpoint, its signing secret and the hosted copy change in one transaction. The service never leaves the list. The copy that served until then is removed 15 seconds later, so calls already in flight to it finish. Audited as `service_build_switched`.
4. **A failure changes nothing for subscribers.** The new copy is removed, VM and address. The serving build keeps serving and stays listed. The failed test is kept with its cases and transcript, and shown in `get_service` as a run with `new_build: true`, `switched: false` and its `outcome` in words. Audited as `service_build_not_switched`. A build that never starts is handled the same way.

For a service in Production, passing conformance is not enough to take over. The new build must also meet the other checks a promotion to Production runs, read for that build: verified by Mynt, no critical or high audit finding, standard terms with their scope, and the licence. A build that passes conformance but fails one of these is removed like a failed one, and its run says which check stopped it.

One new build is tested at a time. Putting another online replaces the one still being tested. Taking the service offline, or archiving it, removes it.

**The new copy's signing secret.** The new copy gets a new secret of its own, not the serving copy's. Code Mynt has not tested yet never holds the secret that authenticates calls to the build subscribers rely on, so a build that leaks its settings cannot be used to forge requests to the serving one. Each build's secret ends with it. This costs nothing in availability: the endpoint and the secret are stored, switched and read together, so every call is signed for the copy it is sent to. The secret reaches the copy as before: a hosted setting in the deploy job's environment, never returned, scrubbed from output.

**The address.** Each copy answers at an address Mynt derives for it, so the service's address changes when Mynt switches to a new build. Nobody types or stores it: Mynt calls the offering's endpoint, which it sets itself.

**If the host does not confirm a removal.** A VM the hosting provider did not confirm as deleted stays on Mynt's record and is tried again at each deploy and on the usage worker's rounds.

### When nothing is serving

A first build, or one put online while the offering is a draft, offline or suspended, goes online in place.

1. `deploy_app` points the offering at it as a draft ("Needs conformance"). An admin's suspension stays as it is.
2. When the build answers, Mynt runs its conformance test itself. It is recorded with no person as its runner, and audited as `service_conformance_after_deploy`.
3. A pass makes the offering `conformance_passed`. For a service in Production it makes it `listed` again, when the build also meets the other production checks above. If it does not, `run_conformance` answers with `not_listed`, the checks that stopped it.
4. A failure leaves it a draft. `run_conformance` runs the test again by hand.

Conformance is always Mynt's own, run from outside the service. Nothing the service or a coding agent runs counts.

### Transcripts

Mynt keeps each run's transcript: for every case, the request it sent (method, path, headers, body), the answer (status and body) and what it expected. This covers real runs, tests of new builds and practice runs. `get_service` returns it on each run as `transcript`.

- Requests are Mynt's fixtures, never a customer's data.
- The signature's digest is left out (`v1=<redacted>`). The signing secret, any credential and anything shaped like one are replaced before the transcript is stored, including in the service's own answers.
- The path is kept, never the address.
- An answer over 8 KB is not kept; the transcript says how long it was.
- A run from before transcripts were kept has `transcript: null` and a `transcript_note` saying so.

## Offline, archive and removal

- **Offline.** `undeploy_app` suspends the offering with the reason ("isn't online"), and products that hand off through it drift. Only an owner or admin of its workspace, at its firm, takes it offline. It is not an admin's suspension: an admin cannot lift it, and it comes back when the service is put online again and passes. A new build being tested beside it is removed too.
- **Archive.** `archive_service { service_id }` takes the offering off the Marketplace and stops calls at once. A new build being tested is removed. Its builds, conformance runs, terms and agreements stay. `archive_service { archived: false }` restores it as a draft, to be put online and tested again. Only an owner or admin of its workspace, at its firm, archives or restores.
- **Removal.** An admin's `remove_app` refuses a service that isn't archived, because suspending its offering as a side effect would pause other firms' products. Once archived, removal unlinks the offering and keeps it as the vendor's and its subscribers' record.

## Reading a service

`get_service { service_id, days? }` returns one service, whole, to any member of its workspace:

| Part | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `stage`, `archived`, `offering`, `hosted` | Where it stands, and the offering's status in words |
| `contract` | The service type's contract, with the input, params and output as field tables (`field`, `type`, `required`, `description`) and the endpoint in full once it is online |
| `new_build` | A new build online beside the serving one while Mynt tests it, or `null` |
| `testing` | Whether builders can test it in the sandbox by its offering id, with the id and how |
| `conformance` | Real runs, tests of new builds that did not take over, and practice runs, newest first, each with its cases, its transcript and the build it tested; whether a test is needed; the build the standing pass ran against |
| `terms` | The current standard terms and every version Mynt knows |
| `subscribers` | Each subscribing firm and app, the terms version accepted, since when, live or sandbox, and the agreement's status |
| `reliability` | Calls, error rate and incidents over the window, from Mynt's own records |
| `activity` | Builds, deploys, stage moves, conformance runs, switches to a new build and terms changes |
| `checklist`, `progress` | What is left, in order |

`subscribers`, `checklist` and `progress` are for the offering firm's own people and Mynt's admins. A member of the workspace who belongs to another firm gets `subscribers: null`, an empty checklist and `firm_only` saying so.

### Reliability

Reliability is read from Mynt's count of calls per subscription and day (`vendor_usage`), its conformance runs and the audit log.

- `calls` and `error_rate` are `null`, with `not_measured` saying why, when nobody has called the service in the window. They are never shown as 0.
- `response_time_ms` is `null` for subscribers' calls: Mynt records whether each call succeeded, not how long it took. `in_last_conformance_run` gives the median and maximum of Mynt's own timed conformance requests.
- `incidents` lists failed conformance runs, new builds that did not take over, times the service went offline, suspensions and archiving.

### The checklist

| Step | Done when |
| --- | --- |
| `vendor_role` | The reader holds the vendor role at the service's firm. Otherwise: ask a Mynt admin |
| `licence` | Only when the service type needs a vendor licence: a verified one is named on the offering |
| `app_online` | The service is online and its offering points at it |
| `service_endpoint` | Mynt's conformance test reached the endpoint and passed. Mynt cannot see inside a build; a `404` at the path says the endpoint isn't in it |
| `practice` | For information, never counted |
| `conformance` | The build that is online passed |
| `terms` | Standard terms with their scope are on file |
| `listed` | The service is in Production |

`get_vendor_onboarding` shows the same steps for a service's offering, with `service` naming it.

## In the Marketplace

Subscribers see a service like any offering: the vendor's name, its terms, its conformance result. Only the vendor's own firm is told that an offering is one of its services built on Mynt (`service` on `list_my_offerings` and on its own rows of `list_vendor_offerings`).

pages.title: Earn & liquidity
pages.markdown:
## Liquidity pools

**Pooled investor capital with withdrawal rights may be a securities offering.** Mynt builds the mechanics only and takes no view on whether a given pool is one. See [The offering gate](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/liquidity-and-treasury.md#the-offering-gate) for what Mynt refuses until a Mynt admin clears a pool.

Liquidity providers are firms or funds that put capital into a product's pools and take it out.

- **Mynt never holds funds.** It records and instructs. The money stays at the licensed partner.
- Every deposit and withdrawal goes only through the [chokepoint](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/money-rails.md#the-chokepoint) on an approved rail of the pool's sponsoring licence provider.
- Customers only ever see dollars. Every figure here is integer US cents.
- A figure that can't be measured is null with a reason, never 0.

The code is `core/src/liquidity.ts`, `core/src/liquidity-tools.ts` and `core/src/liquidity-schema.ts`.

### The offering gate

Real (non-sandbox) commitments are refused, by a hard gate on the deposit path, until a Mynt admin sets the pool's `offering_cleared` flag with `set_pool_offering_cleared`. That records who cleared it and the legal basis (`offering_cleared_by`, `offering_legal_basis`). The refusal (`offering_not_cleared`) says why.

- Sandbox pools move no real money and aren't subject to the gate.
- Someone at the pool's product firm or its licence provider can't set the flag, even with the admin role.
- An uncleared real pool isn't listed to liquidity providers.

### A pool

A pool belongs to one product component. The product's builder creates it (`create_pool`), for a component with an approved sponsorship. It is in US dollars.

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Status | `open`, `paused` or `closed` |
| Minimum reserve | `min_reserve_bps` of obligations (10000 = 100%, rounded up), plus `min_reserve_floor_cents` |
| Notice period | In days. 0 is allowed |
| Commitment limits | `min_commitment_cents` and `max_commitment_cents` per firm, counted against the firm's settled net position plus what is still on its way in |

A pool is paused until the component's licence provider approves it (`approve_pool`) and names its rails:

- an approved `deposit` or `on_ramp` rail and an approved `payout` or `off_ramp` rail, both the licence provider's own;
- every state the deposit rail serves must also be served by the payout rail, so capital that came in can get out.

A pool uses the rails named at approval and no other. It doesn't follow a replacement if one is revoked.

Sandbox pools (`sandbox: true`) run the same mechanics on sandbox ledger rows. A sandbox commitment gives no access to the product's health figures, so it can't be a way into a real product's books.

### Commitments and capital

`commit_to_pool` takes an amount and the US state the capital moves from. The firm states it, as a customer states `residence_state`, and the rail must serve it.

- The state can't change while the firm holds a position, and only takes effect once a deposit is authorised.
- A pool's licence provider or its product's firm can't be a liquidity provider in it.
- The call reserves a deposit under the pool's lock, checks the limits, and asks the chokepoint.
