| `request_mainnet_review` | Builder | Asks for a review. Takes the `program_id` of a mainnet program and the `build_id` of a succeeded build |
| `get_mainnet_review` | Builder | Status, step, every check's result, the findings, cost, decision, an upgrade's timelock, and the review's own audit log |
| `cancel_mainnet_review` | Builder | Cancels a review |
| `list_mainnet_reviews` | Mynt admin | Lists reviews |
| `approve_mainnet_program` | Mynt admin | Approves. Its answer shows the whole report again. `allow_exceptions` must name every exception the review lists |
| `reject_mainnet_program` | Mynt admin | Rejects |

A program has one open review at a time. A partial unique index enforces it, whatever races.

Reviews are stored in `solana_mainnet_reviews` with an append-only `solana_mainnet_review_log`. Every request, approval, rejection and cancellation is also in Mynt's audit log.

#### What the gate reviews

Mynt's verify build keeps three things next to the bytes, read back and hashed by Mynt. A build made before this capture existed has none of them and can't pass: build it again.

##### The workspace exactly as it went into the build container

The build archives the workspace once, feeds that very archive to the build container, and keeps it (`solana_program_sources`): text files as text, others as base64, links as links.

- The archive holds every file type, dot-folders such as `.cargo/` included, and nested `target/` or `node_modules/` folders included.
- Only the top-level `target/`, `node_modules/` and `.anchor/` are left out, as the container copy always did.
- A workspace over 16 MB fails the build. Nothing is ever silently left out.

A workspace that ships build output fails the build too, with the paths named:

- a cargo target folder at any depth below the top level: a folder named `target` that holds cargo's `.rustc_info.json` or `CACHEDIR.TAG`. A source module folder that happens to be called `target` is fine;
- a folder named `docker-target` or `.anchor`;
- cargo's `.fingerprint/` folders;
- `*.rlib`, `*.rmeta`, `*.d` or `*.so` files;
- a file name with control characters.

Cargo's target dir in the build and IDL containers is `/mynt-target`, outside the source and empty when the build starts. So nothing shipped can pass for a "fresh" artifact cargo would reuse instead of compiling. The programs, dep-info and IDL are read only from there.

This holds for every build, devnet included: Mynt compiles every program itself.

##### Every dependency the build used

`solana_program_deps` holds:

- each crate of the `Cargo.lock` the build compiled with, its source and its checksum;
- the sha256 of the `.crate` cargo downloaded in the fetch container (before any of the builder's code ran), compared with that checksum;
- the full source of every crate not on the crate allowlist (up to 16 MB);
- the `Cargo.lock` itself.

##### The IDL built in Mynt's own offline container

The IDL is built in a third container with no network. It gets a fresh copy of the same source and crates after the programs are out, so `anchor idl build` (which runs the workspace's code) can't touch them.

The test run's IDL, built on the host by the workspace's own code, is kept only to name events and never replaces it.

#### Hard rules

The hard rules (`core/src/solana/program-rules.ts`) are driven by the [vulnerability database](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/solana-programs.md#vulnerability-database). They are deterministic, run by Mynt in-process when the review is requested, with no model.

- Entries whose gate is `block` refuse the program.
- `flag` entries are recorded as leads the audit agent must confirm or dismiss.
- A finding names the entry's id, what was found, where, and by which signal.

The rug-pull entries are these.

##### No value-moving programs for now

Refused:

- references to `anchor_spl::token`, `token_2022`, `token_interface`, `associated_token`, `spl_token`, `spl_token_2022` or `spl_associated_token_account`;
- token CPIs: `transfer`, `transfer_checked`, `mint_to`, `burn`, `approve`, `set_authority`, `close_account`;
- system-program transfers and assigns (`system_program::transfer`, `system_instruction::transfer`/`assign`, `SystemInstruction::Transfer`), with a note when the file signs CPIs with the program's own PDAs;
- lamports moved by hand: `sub_lamports`, `add_lamports`, `lamports.borrow_mut()`.

##### No hidden admin

Refused:

- an `#[account(address = …)]`, `constraint` or `owner` constraint, a `require!`/`require_keys_eq!`, or an `==`/`!=` comparison against a hard-coded key (`pubkey!`, `Pubkey::from_str`, `Pubkey::new_from_array`, or a `const` holding one; well-known program and sysvar ids aside);
- an authority, admin or owner field set to anything but the key of an account that signs that instruction (an argument, a non-signer account). `Pubkey::default()` to renounce is fine;
- an Anchor `close = target` whose target doesn't sign.

A hard-coded key equal to Mynt's own mainnet signer is noted, not refused. No program should need it.

##### The upgrade authority stays with Mynt's mainnet signer

The upgrade authority is the `mainnet-vault` key or Turnkey custody (`custody-service`). For an upgrade, the program's recorded authority must be that signer.

While mainnet's signer isn't configured this is `pending`. It is asserted again at approval and when the deploy or upgrade starts. The deployer also refuses any other backend on mainnet.

##### Three ways of looking

Each rule looks three ways, because each alone can be fooled.

| Signal | What it reads |
| --- | --- |
| Source | The captured Rust with comments stripped. A comment can neither hide code nor create a finding |
| IDL | Instructions taking a token program (by its fixed address or name) or a token account, and accounts pinned to a fixed address that must sign |
| Bytes | The SPL Token, Token-2022 and Associated Token program ids embedded in the sBPF program, raw or as base58 text, plus the 32 bytes of any hard-coded key the source checks against, as corroboration |

Limits, returned with every result:

- The source scan is pattern-based, not a compiler. Macro-generated code, hand-built CPI bytes or an authority passed through more than one variable can be missed.
- The IDL is built by the workspace's own code and shows only what Anchor records.
- The bytes show only ids the program embeds. The System Program's id is all zeros, so system transfers are invisible there.

Without captured source a program is refused.

#### What the rules read

The rules read what the compiler read. The authority is rustc's own dep-info.

After the build, Mynt streams the stopped build container's `/workdir` and unpacked crates out as tar (hashed, never unpacked). It keeps every dep-info file cargo wrote (`/mynt-target/**/*.d`, outside build scripts' `out/` folders) with the sha256 of the container's copy of every workspace and registry file, and of every file in each downloaded `.crate` (`solana_program_depinfo`).

The review refuses a build when:

- a file the compiler read is missing from the captured workspace, or differs from it (something rewrote it during the build);
- a file the compiler read isn't in its crate's `.crate`, or differs;
- a file belongs to a crate not in the `Cargo.lock`;
- a file lies outside the workspace and the crates.io registry cache;
- a file is in the target dir, other than in a build script's `out/` folder of a crate in the `Cargo.lock` or of a workspace crate whose build script is an exception;
- a dep-info line isn't a rule, or a path has control characters;
- the build has no dep-info record.

The rules then read exactly the workspace files listed, wherever they are (a real module under `tests/` or a nested `target/` included).

- Files generated by a workspace crate's build script are listed as exceptions.
- When any build-time code ran (a workspace build script or proc macro, or a dependency's build script, which is nearly always), the rules also read every captured `.rs` file, not only dep-info's list.
- A hit that would block in a file dep-info doesn't list (an integration test under `tests/`, say) doesn't refuse the review. It becomes an exception, `uncompiled-hit:<file>`, that the approving admin must name. The deploy-time re-check refuses any such hit the approval didn't name.
- Manifest patterns (such as `overflow-checks`) read every captured `Cargo.toml`.

Residual risk: dep-info is written in the same container where build scripts and proc macros run, so such code could rewrite a `.d` file. Any compiled file whose contents changed is still refused, and reading every captured `.rs` file covers what a rewritten `.d` could hide from the workspace. A dependency's build script is trusted by being on the allowlist or named by an admin.

##### Module resolution as a cross-check

Mynt's own module resolution is only a cross-check. It takes crate roots from the manifests, read with a real TOML parser (`smol-toml` 1.9.1, so dotted keys and inline tables mean what they mean to cargo), then follows `mod`, `#[path]` and `include!`.

- Wherever it disagrees with dep-info, in either direction, that is an exception (`module-tree-mismatch:<file>`) the admin must name, and the review's caveats say so.
- A module path chosen by `cfg_attr(..., path = ...)` is always an exception, and the resolver follows every candidate.
- A manifest that isn't valid TOML is an exception too.

#### Exceptions

What can change the build beyond the reviewed source is listed as **exceptions**, each with an id. A Mynt admin must name every one in `allow_exceptions` to approve. The review still runs every gate, so the admin decides with the full report.

Exceptions:

- a `.cargo/config` or `.cargo/config.toml` anywhere in the workspace with any setting beyond the template's `[resolver] incompatible-rust-versions = "fallback"` (which Mynt's build sets by environment anyway);
- a build script in any package;
- a procedural-macro crate in the workspace;
- `[patch]` or `[replace]`;
- `include!`, `include_str!` or `include_bytes!` of a file that isn't Rust text, or of a path that isn't a plain string (`concat!(env!("OUT_DIR"), ...)`);
- `#[path]` to a non-`.rs` file;
- a `mod` whose file isn't in the workspace (generated at build time);
- links.

A `rust-toolchain.toml` isn't an exception. The build pins `RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN` by environment, which outranks it, and `cargo build-sbf` compiles with the platform tools' own Rust.

#### Dependencies

Every crate must come from crates.io. A git or other-registry source, or a path dependency outside the captured workspace, is refused. The crate the build used must match `Cargo.lock`'s checksum.

A crate on `core/schemas/solana-crate-allowlist.json` passes.

- The list holds exact names only (crates.io has no namespaces).
- It is generated from the template's `Cargo.lock`. CI fails if the template resolves a crate that isn't on it.
- It is changed only by a reviewed pull request.
- Allowing a crate by name trusts whoever owns it on crates.io. A new release they publish is accepted once a `Cargo.lock` resolves it: checksum-verified and cargo-audited, but not reviewed line by line. So the list stays short, and an Anchor or Solana upgrade means reviewing it again.
- It also lists crates that are never allowed, because they move value: `anchor-spl`, `spl-token`, `spl-token-2022`, `spl-associated-token-account`.

Any other crate is an exception (`crate:<name>@<version>`) an admin must name. The hard rules run over its source too: a blocking finding there refuses the program. The auditor gets those crates' source beside the program's.

#### The IDL

The IDL is used only if every instruction it lists is in the program's bytes: its 8-byte discriminator, as stored data, a 64-bit load, or two 32-bit immediates. An IDL naming an instruction the program doesn't have refuses the review.

The agents and Mynt's PoC re-run get it with the builder's free text neutralised: no doc strings, error messages or constant values, and names cut to 64 characters.

An instruction the IDL leaves out can't be found this way, which every review says.

#### Vulnerability database

The database is `core/schemas/solana-vulnerabilities.json`, version 2, read by `core/src/solana/vuln-db.ts`. It has one entry per vulnerability class:

- id, title, severity, category and gate (`block` or `flag`);
- a description;
- detections;
- public references: incident write-ups, the Sealevel attacks, Trail of Bits' not-so-smart-contracts, Neodyme, Helius, the crates' docs;
- a bad and a good fixture under `core/test/fixtures/`.

Detections:

| Detection | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `source_pattern` | A regular expression over the comment-stripped Rust, with an optional `unless` that clears a file, an `absent` pattern, or a named built-in analysis |
| `idl_shape` | A shape in the IDL |
| `bytecode_program_ref` | Program ids in the bytes |
| `dependency_advisory` | cargo-audit's RustSec findings |
| `red_team_scenario` | How to attack it, for the agents |

`core/test/mainnet-gate.test.js` checks every entry against both fixtures. Its detections must catch the bad one and pass the good one, and the template program must trigger none.

The audit and red-team agents get the whole database in their sandboxes (`job/vulnerabilities.json`) as their checklist.

- a function that calls `.unload()` after a CPI in a file that uses `LazyAccount`.

It blocks on mainnet. On devnet, `deploy_program` and `upgrade_program` still deploy and return the same findings as `warnings`, saying mainnet would refuse the program.

##### Changing the database

- Mynt admins see the database with `list_vulnerability_rules` and suggest entries with `propose_vulnerability_rule`, which checks the entry's shape and stores it as a proposal (`solana_vuln_rule_proposals`).
- Only a pull request that adds the entry with its fixtures changes the database.
- `core/scripts/vuln-db-suggest.mjs [--since YYYY-MM-DD]` turns new RustSec advisories (through OSV) against Solana, Anchor, SPL, crypto and serialization crates into suggested entries for that review. It never edits the file.

##### A new version re-checks what is deployed

When the server starts on a higher database version, the gate's worker runs the new hard rules on every deployed mainnet program: its stored bytes, IDL and captured source.

A program that fails is flagged (`solana_program_flags`):

- its firm gets `program.review_flagged`;
- Mynt admins see it in `list_program_flags` and `ops_status`;
- its upgrades (requests, approved and scheduled ones) wait until an admin records a review with `resolve_program_flag`.

The program keeps running. Mynt never takes one down.

#### White-box audit

The audit runs in a fresh sandbox of Mynt's that gets only the captured source.

##### Static analysis

Each tool is pinned by sha256:

- [cargo-audit](https://github.com/rustsec/rustsec) 0.22.2 (the release binary) against the RustSec advisory database, fetched fresh each run, for the `Cargo.lock` the build compiled with;
- [Radar](https://github.com/Auditware/radar) (Auditware; GPL-3.0, run, not vendored) at commit `3439053`, its source tarball by sha256 and its four images by digest.

Radar honours `radar-disable` comments in what it scans, so Mynt removes them from its copy first.

What blocks:

- a tool that couldn't run;
- a cargo-audit vulnerability;
- a Radar critical or high finding of medium or high certainty.

Radar's low-certainty findings go to the audit agent as leads.

`PROGRAM_GATE_CARGO_AUDIT_IGNORE` (comma-separated `RUSTSEC-YYYY-NNNN` ids) lets the operator accept an advisory that can't reach an on-chain program. It is shown in every report.

##### The program-audit agent

The program-audit agent (`core/workspaces/program-audit/`) runs in the same sandbox after Mynt has read the tools' results.

- It reads the source, Mynt's hard-rule results and the static findings, and writes JSON findings with a severity and a quote.
- Mynt checks each quote against the named file. A finding whose quote isn't there is kept, marked unverified, and never blocks.
- A verified critical or high finding blocks, and so does an audit that didn't finish.
- It never sees the builder agent's conversation.

#### Black-box red team

The red team (`core/workspaces/program-red-team/`) runs in a sandbox of its own that gets only the exact bytes Mynt stored and the IDL, never the source.

It runs the pinned toolchain's `solana-test-validator` with the program at its address and writes attacks: wrong signer, account substitution, PDA spoofing, authority takeover, draining, re-initialization, arithmetic edges.

A finding counts only with a proof of concept (PoC): a folder with `run.sh`, run in two phases.

1. `setup` creates a victim with keys of its own and writes `claim.json`: the victim's signer keys and accounts.
2. `attack` writes `attack.json`: its transactions' signatures.

Mynt reads the PoCs back as text and re-runs each in a third, fresh sandbox, on a fresh validator of its own, never the agent's. It snapshots the victim's accounts itself between the phases and after.

An exploit is **confirmed** only when:

- every attack transaction succeeded on Mynt's validator, invoked the program, and was signed by none of the victim's keys; and
- a victim account the program owns, which held a victim key or had lamports, changed or lost lamports.

Outcomes:

- A confirmed exploit blocks.
- Findings without a PoC, or whose PoC doesn't confirm (a failed transaction, a denial of service), are reported and don't block.
- A red team that didn't finish blocks.
- If Mynt can't complete its re-run, the review fails and can be requested again.

Trident (Ackee's Anchor fuzzer) isn't run. It fuzzes a program from its source through a hand-written harness, which would put source in front of the black-box red team and make the harness agent-written. The red team's PoCs cover the same ground against the real bytes.

#### Sign-off and timelock

When every automated gate passes, the review waits for a Mynt admin (`awaiting_approval`).

`get_mainnet_review` and the approval itself say plainly what the gate can't promise (`caveats`):

- a clean audit or red-team result isn't proof;
- the local validator can't show behaviour depending on time or slot, on live mainnet state (oracles, other programs), on the cluster (feature gates, compute, fees), on transaction ordering under load, or on later upgrades;
- IDL-omitted instructions aren't checked;
- every exception, with what was allowed.

**A first deploy** then goes ahead with `deploy_program` for exactly that build, within `MAINNET_APPROVAL_TTL_DAYS` (default 14) of the approval.

**An upgrade:**

- is announced at once to the firm's webhooks (`program.upgrade_scheduled`, with the hash and when it can run);
- runs only after `MAINNET_UPGRADE_TIMELOCK_HOURS` (default 48) and an admin's approval. Mynt starts it itself when both hold, as the builder who asked;
- must start within `MAINNET_APPROVAL_TTL_DAYS` after its timelock ends.

Upgrades need an admin too because an upgrade can turn a reviewed program into anything, and the timelock only helps users who are watching.

The builder or an admin can cancel until the upgrade starts. A cancelled or rejected upgrade goes out as `program.upgrade_cancelled`.

A review becomes `executed` once the program holds exactly the reviewed bytes.

#### An approval is used once

`deploy_program` and `upgrade_program` (and Mynt's own start of a timelocked upgrade) check the approval first, then claim it atomically, last, just before the deploy starts (`started`). Two deploys at once can't both use it, and a cancel can't race it.

- The claim re-runs the current vulnerability database's hard rules over exactly those bytes and refuses if a newer version blocks them.
- The claim is given back only if the deploy couldn't start, or if the attempt ended with the program unchanged.
- If the program ended up holding another build, the review fails.

So going A, then B, then A again needs a fresh review (and, for an upgrade, a fresh announcement and timelock).

If a first deploy finds an earlier build of the program already on mainnet (a lost confirmation), Mynt records that build and stops. The new one needs a review as an upgrade.

#### Review statuses

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `running` | The automated gates are running. Its step is `analysis_provisioning`, `analysis`, `audit`, `red_provisioning`, `red_team`, `confirm_provisioning` or `confirming` |
| `awaiting_approval` | Waiting for a Mynt admin |
| `approved` | A Mynt admin approved it; no deploy or upgrade has claimed the approval yet |
| `started` | The approval was claimed and the deploy or upgrade started |
| `executed` | The program holds exactly the reviewed bytes |
| `blocked` | An automated gate blocked it |
| `rejected` | A Mynt admin rejected it |
| `cancelled` | The builder or a Mynt admin cancelled it |
| `failed` | The review couldn't be completed (for example Mynt's re-run of the proofs of concept), or the program ended up holding another build |

#### Budget

Both agents reach the model only through Mynt's agent proxy, which meters every call against their own caps.

| Setting | Default | What it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PROGRAM_AUDIT_CAP_USD` | 5 | The audit agent's cap |
| `PROGRAM_RED_TEAM_CAP_USD` | 8 | The red team's cap |
| `PROGRAM_GATE_MODEL` | The builds' model | The model both use |
| `PROGRAM_ANALYSIS_MINUTES` | 45 | Time limit for static analysis |
| `PROGRAM_AUDIT_MINUTES` | 45 | Time limit for the audit |
| `PROGRAM_RED_TEAM_MINUTES` | 60 | Time limit for the red team |
| `PROGRAM_GATE_MONTHLY_CAP_USD` | 100 | Caps all reviews in a month |

Each review reserves its two caps from a per-month counter, updated atomically only while it stays under the monthly cap, and gives back what it didn't spend once its agents are done.

A review's cost is its sandboxes' machine time plus both agents' metered spend. Mynt pays it, like the build audit.

#### Retention

What a build captures for this gate (its source, its dependencies, and what the compiler read) is kept for any build a mainnet review names or a program version was deployed from.

The rest, such as devnet builds nobody took further, is deleted once older than `PROGRAM_SOURCE_RETENTION_DAYS` (default 30). Such a build must be built again before a mainnet review.

#### Gate skills

The agents' skills are vendored verbatim from GitHub with their licences (`UPSTREAM.json`):

- The program-audit agent follows [exvulsec/exvul-solana-skill](https://github.com/exvulsec/exvul-solana-skill) (MIT), with the account-validation, CPI, PDA, account-lifecycle, instruction-introspection and centralization-risk skills from [PlamenTSV/plamen](https://github.com/PlamenTSV/plamen) (MIT).
- The red team uses Plamen's verification-protocol, account-validation and PDA skills.

#### An outside audit

`smart_contract_audit` is a US service type, so audit firms can offer it as vendors (`create_vendor_offering`). The builder engages and pays the auditor directly. Mynt only lists it, and it doesn't replace the gate.

#### The gate in CI

CI's `solana-program` job runs the hard rules and the static analysis on the template program as Mynt captured it (they pass) and the hard rules on a token-vault fixture (refused).

pages.title: Confidential computing
pages.markdown:
This file covers what Mynt's confidential service protects, the three confidential hosts, how the service's keys and attestation work, how releases are announced, the settings by name, and the operator's steps on each cloud. It is for licence providers' engineers, operators and Mynt admins.

See also: [Firms, licences and licence providers](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/licence-providers.md), [Connecting a licence provider to Mynt](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/partners.md), [Running Mynt](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/operations.md), [Mynt architecture](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/architecture.md).

Some of what Mynt keeps shouldn't be readable even by whoever runs Mynt's server: a licence provider's books, the vault's root key, and the keys that sign what Mynt attests. They go to a **confidential host**: a small service (`deploy/confidential`, code name "keyhouse") that runs in hardware-isolated memory whose exact image the hardware measures and signs for.

In this file, "partner" means the licence provider, as in the partner kit and the partner ledger.

## What is protected

The table compares a server on the `local` host with one whose confidential service is deployed and whose migration has run.

| | Until the service is deployed (`local`) | Once it is, and the migration has run |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A partner's live books | Read in the clear by Mynt's server, then encrypted per product | Sealed by the partner to the service's attested key; opened, checked and computed only inside it. One product's figures and a signature over their fingerprint come out |
| The vault's root (`MYNT_VAULT_KEY`) | In the server's environment file | Adopted by the service, never released, and removed from the server |
| Values in the vault | Sealed with `MYNT_VAULT_KEY` | Re-wrapped to a data key the service releases into the server's memory at boot, never written to its disk |
| Keys derived from the vault (MACs, on-chain subject hashes, sandbox keys) | From `MYNT_VAULT_KEY` | Exactly the same keys, from HKDF-Extract of the root, which the service releases; the root itself stays inside |
| The health attester key | None | An Ed25519 key derived inside the enclave from the service's root, so it exists only where the root does. It signs every snapshot the service computes, and nothing else: no caller can have it sign a message |
| Who can use the service's keys | Not applicable | Only an enclave running the exact announced image (its PCR0), out of debug mode: no person, Mynt's operators and the parent instance included |

On Confidential Space the health attester is a Cloud KMS `EC_SIGN_ED25519` key only the attested image can use.

## Hosts

Mynt's server reaches the confidential service through one brand-neutral interface, `ConfidentialHost` (`core/src/confidential/host.ts`):

- `attest(nonce)` and `measurements()`;
- `seal` and `unseal(purpose, bytes, context)`;
- `sign(key, bytes)` and `publicKey(name)`;
- `computeHealth`;
- the vault's `adoptVaultRoot` and `releaseVaultKeys`.

`CONFIDENTIAL_HOST` chooses one of three adapters:

| `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST` | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `local` (the default) | In Mynt's own process, keyed by `MYNT_VAULT_KEY`. For development, tests, and every server until the operator deploys the service |
| `aws-nitro` (the documented deployment) | The service in an AWS Nitro Enclave |
| `gcp-confidential-space` | The same service as a Google Cloud Confidential Space container, kept as an alternative |

Notes on each:

- **`local`** keeps the same rules but protects nothing from whoever runs the server, and its attestation says so (`format: "none"`, `attested: false`). It is what an unset `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST` means, and the server says so in two places: one line when it starts, and `ops_status`, which reads `Confidential host: local (keys sealed in this server's own process)`.
- **`aws-nitro`**: a Nitro Enclave is an isolated VM carved out of an EC2 instance, with no network, disk or console. The Nitro hypervisor measures its image file into PCRs, and its security module signs attestation documents over them. Only `core/src/confidential/aws-nitro.ts` names the provider.
- **`gcp-confidential-space`**: an AMD SEV-SNP or Intel TDX confidential VM. Only `core/src/confidential/gcp-confidential-space.ts` and `attestation-verify.ts` name that provider.

Both remote adapters share `core/src/confidential/remote.ts` (the connection, the pin, every request) and differ only in how they check an attestation.

The local host is never a fallback:

- A server set to a remote host that is misconfigured, unreachable or fails its attestation gets an error, at start-up or on the request. Nothing is sealed, signed or opened in the server's own process in its place.
- A server with any `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST_*` setting but no `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST` refuses to start, rather than run on the local host with a confidential service half configured.

### What a sealed value is bound to

Every sealed value is bound to the host that sealed it and to its purpose, so it never opens on another host or as another purpose. A value sealed with a `context` is bound to that too. The platform key vault seals each key with its key type as the context, so a sealed key moved to another type's row in the database doesn't open there.

Keys the vault sealed before contexts existed still open. Each is sealed again, bound to its type, the first time the server opens it, and every new or replaced key is bound from the start.

## How the enclave's keys work

This section describes AWS KMS, which the `aws-nitro` host uses.

### The root and the wrap key

The service's root is a random 32-byte key that AWS KMS generates (`GenerateDataKey`). It exists outside the enclave only wrapped by one symmetric KMS key, the wrap key.

Every KMS call the enclave makes carries, as `Recipient`, a fresh attestation document whose public key is an RSA key made inside the enclave. KMS checks the document's signature and PCRs against the key policy and answers in `CiphertextForRecipient`, never in plaintext. That answer is CMS enveloped data encrypted to the RSA key, opened by `deploy/confidential/src/cms.mjs`.

### The key policy

The key policy (`deploy/confidential/aws/key-policy.json`; the CloudFormation template makes the same one) has six statements:

1. The account may manage the key but not use it, and not change this policy.
2. One named role, the break-glass role, may change the policy (`kms:PutKeyPolicy`). It can't use the key either.
3. **Everyone else** is denied `kms:PutKeyPolicy`, whatever their IAM permissions say.
4. The instance's role may call `kms:Decrypt` and `kms:GenerateDataKey` only when `kms:RecipientAttestation:ImageSha384` (PCR0) is the release's.
5. **Everyone** is denied those calls when it isn't. That includes any call with no attestation at all, whatever their IAM permissions say.
6. Nobody may re-encrypt, encrypt, or create grants on it.

What follows from it:

- The parent instance has the role's credentials (it relays them to the enclave from the instance metadata service). It still can't use the key itself, and couldn't read KMS's answer if it relayed one.
- A debug-mode enclave reports all-zero PCRs and is refused the same way.
- The policy is what names the PCR0 that may use the key, so whoever can rewrite it can admit an image of their own. Only the break-glass role can, and it is used for one thing: updating the allowed PCR0 at an upgrade. Nobody should hold it day to day.

### The alarm on the key

The CloudFormation template sets up an alarm on the wrap key. It sends an email whenever the key's policy is changed, or the key is disabled, scheduled for deletion or granted:

- an EventBridge rule matches those calls on this key in CloudTrail and sends the call itself (who made it, when, from where) to an SNS topic;
- a CloudWatch alarm on that rule goes into alarm on the first match;
- a CloudTrail trail recording management events is what the rule hears through. The template creates one unless told the account already has one.

AWS emails the alarm's address once to confirm it. Until the link in that email is clicked, the alarm is silent.

The only expected alarm is the planned change of the allowed PCR0 at an upgrade. Treat any other as the service's keys being exposed: stop sending it anything, and tell partners.

### What the key policy can't do

The AWS account's administrators can still rewrite the key policy. They can't do it as themselves, but whoever administers the account's IAM can change who may assume the break-glass role, assume it, and then change the policy. An account's root user can do the same.

So the policy change is made loud and narrow, not impossible:

- it takes a second, deliberate step (taking over one named role) that leaves its own CloudTrail record;
- it raises the alarm;
- it doesn't change what partners and Mynt's server check: the attested PCRs, the wrap key's ARN and the client authority. An enclave from another image is refused by both whatever the policy says.

What a rewritten policy does allow is an image of the attacker's own to unwrap the service's root, and so to open what is sealed under it. Nothing in the account prevents that. Only keeping the account's administrators few, the break-glass role unheld, and the alarm watched does.

The enclave calls KMS directly: Signature Version 4 with the role's temporary credentials, TLS end to end through AWS's `vsock-proxy` on the parent, with no SDK.

### The health attester and Ed25519

The root is protected because the two KMS calls it uses, `GenerateDataKey` and `Decrypt`, carry the enclave's attestation document as their `Recipient`, and the key policy admits only this image's. KMS signing can't be gated on attestation in that way, so a KMS signing key would be usable by the parent instance's role directly (`deploy/confidential/src/nitro.mjs`). AWS's KMS documentation lists the calls that accept an attestation document; check it before changing this design.

The enclave therefore derives its Ed25519 attester from its root (HKDF, as the local host does). The attester exists only inside an attested enclave and is the same after every restart.

Partners check its public key the same way as the rest: it is bound into every attestation.

The attester signs in one place only: at the end of the health check, over the fingerprint of the report that check just computed. It is not a signing key a caller can use:

- `POST /v1/sign` refuses it for every caller (`reserved_key`), before the policy is even read, and `policy.json` doesn't list it. Mynt's server can read its public key and nothing more.
- The local host and both adapters refuse it the same way.

So a signature by the attester always means that the measured image opened a statement, checked it and computed that report. The report says what was checked: see [Sealed statements and snapshots](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/confidential-computing.md#sealed-statements-and-snapshots).

## What partners check

`GET /confidential/attestation?nonce=<16 to 64 URL-safe characters>` (public, one a second) returns the service's own answer, relayed unchanged, with the releases Mynt has announced.

### An attestation from an enclave

From an enclave the answer has `format: "nitro-cose"`, and `token` is the attestation document (COSE_Sign1, base64). In the document:

- `nonce` is the caller's nonce;
- `user_data` is `mynt-keys-<sha256>` over the keys returned beside it;
- `public_key` is the service's TLS key.

The keys returned beside it are the service's TLS key, the ingest key partners seal to, the health attester's public key, and `config`, the settings the enclave was handed by its parent instance:

| `config` | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `kms_key` | The ARN of the KMS key that wraps the service's root |
| `region` | That key's region |
| `client_ca_sha256` | The SHA-256 of the one authority whose client certificates the service accepts: who may call it |

The parent instance isn't trusted, and these three reach the enclave from it. So the enclave binds them into every attestation with its keys, and a verifier must be given the value it expects for each. An attestation is refused when a value differs, when the enclave binds none, or when the verifier has nothing to compare it with.

That is what stops someone with root on the parent from handing the enclave a client authority of their own and calling it as Mynt's server: the enclave would attest that authority, and Mynt's server and partners would refuse it.

### Checking it with the verify script

`core/scripts/verify-mynt-enclave.mjs --url … --expected-pcr0 … --expected-pcr1 … --expected-pcr2 … --expected-kms-key <arn> --expected-client-ca-sha256 <64 hex>` checks the attestation with nothing but Node. It checks:

- the COSE ES384 signature with the document's certificate;
- that certificate's chain, through the document's own bundle, up to the AWS Nitro Enclaves root certificate pinned in `aws-nitro.ts`, each certificate valid now;
- that the document was made in the last five minutes;
- PCR0, PCR1 and PCR2 equal to the ones published for the release, and not a debug-mode enclave's zeros;
- its own fresh nonce;
- both bindings;
- the wrap key's ARN and the client authority's SHA-256, each equal to the one given.

`--expected-kms-key` and `--expected-client-ca-sha256` are required. Without them the script stops before checking anything: an honest image whose root is wrapped by a key someone else controls, or which someone other than Mynt's server may call, would otherwise pass.

Mynt gives a partner both values when it onboards, and they don't change from one release to the next. A partner keeps the ones it was first given and asks why if the script ever reports another.

The pinned root certificate is `AWS_NitroEnclaves_Root-G1`, from AWS's `AWS_NitroEnclaves_Root-G1.zip`, never fetched from Mynt. Its SHA-256 fingerprint is:

`64:1A:03:21:A3:E2:44:EF:E4:56:46:31:95:D6:06:31:7E:D7:CD:CC:3C:17:56:E0:98:93:F3:C6:8F:79:BB:5B`

### A Confidential Space deployment

For a Confidential Space deployment the script checks an OIDC token instead, with `--expected-digest sha256:…`. It checks:

- the token's RS256 signature against the attestation service's published keys;
- `swname` `CONFIDENTIAL_SPACE`, `STABLE`, secure boot, and `dbgstat` `disabled-since-boot`;
- the image digest;
- the nonce and the key binding in `eat_nonce`;
- the key custody the service binds with its keys (`config`), each value required: `--expected-wrap-key` (the Cloud KMS key that wraps its root), `--expected-signing-key health-attester=<key version>` (once for each signing key; the service may offer no other), and `--expected-client-ca-sha256`.

On Confidential Space those names reach the workload from the VM's metadata, outside the measured image, so whoever runs the VM could point an honest image at keys of their own. The token alone doesn't show that. The bound settings do, and Mynt's server requires the same three (`CONFIDENTIAL_HOST_WRAP_KEY`, `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST_SIGNING_KEYS`, `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST_CLIENT_CA`).

### Sealed statements and snapshots

[Connecting a licence provider to Mynt](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/partners.md) has the partner's steps, including sealing a live statement (`mynt.sealed_statement.v1`: X25519, HKDF-SHA256, AES-256-GCM, with the firm, environment and request bound as associated data).

A snapshot computed by the service shows `enclave: { public_key, signature_ok }` in `list_product_health`. Mynt's server recomputes the fingerprint and checks the signature before it stores anything. See [Product health](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/licence-providers.md#product-health).

The report the service computes carries `sealed_statement`, which says what the service checked. It is part of the report, so the fingerprint the attester signs covers it:

| Field | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `result` | `ok`, or the code of the check that failed (the figures are then unavailable) |
| `signer_public_key` | The key whose signature over the statement verified, or null when none did |
| `as_of` | The statement's own clock |
| `checked` | What the statement was held to: the firm (`entity_id`), `environment`, `request_id`, the firm's registered `public_key`, `max_age_ms`, and the clock its freshness was judged against (`now`) |

Mynt's server refuses a report that doesn't say it checked the statement Mynt asked about, or that gives figures without a statement the firm's registered key signed.

## How Mynt's server trusts the service

The connection is TLS 1.3 with a certificate on each side:

- Mynt presents a client certificate (`CONFIDENTIAL_HOST_CLIENT_CERT`, `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST_CLIENT_KEY`: paths to files, made by `deploy/confidential/make-client-cert.sh`) from the one authority the service trusts. The same script writes that authority's certificate, `ca.crt`, which `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST_CLIENT_CA` points at. Its private key is deleted as soon as the client certificate is issued, so no other certificate can come from it.
- The service presents a key it made inside the enclave at boot, which no authority vouches for.

Before anything is sent, Mynt:

1. fetches an attestation over a connection to the service;
2. checks it as a partner would, with the PCRs required to be a release in effect in Mynt's record, the wrap key required to be `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST_KMS_KEY`, and the client authority the service accepts required to be the one in `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST_CLIENT_CA`;
3. pins the TLS key the attestation binds.

A connection presenting any other key is closed before a byte is written. The pin lasts ten minutes.

On the parent instance the TLS connection is relayed byte for byte (TCP 8443 to the enclave's vsock port 8443), so the parent sees ciphertext only.

The service allows each caller (by certificate common name) only what `deploy/confidential/policy.json` lists, and that file is part of the measured image. What is sealed for `vault-legacy-root`, `vault-keys`, `signing-key` or `partner-ledger` has no endpoint that returns it.

A common name only means something because one authority issues the certificates. The service accepts exactly one authority certificate (a bundle of several is refused at start-up) and attests its SHA-256, as [An attestation from an enclave](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/confidential-computing.md#an-attestation-from-an-enclave) describes.

## Inside the enclave

### An enclave keeps nothing across restarts

`mynt confidential init` asks a new service to make its root. It stores the wrapped form (ciphertext only an attested enclave can unwrap) in Mynt's database (`confidential_keys`, `host-root`).

Whenever the enclave restarts, Mynt's server hands the wrapped root back (`POST /v1/unlock`) after attesting the new enclave, so the operator has nothing to copy.

Keep a copy of the printed wrapped root somewhere safe as well. Without it and the database, what is sealed under the root can't be opened.

### The service and its helper

The service is Node with no npm dependencies. The enclave has only vsock, which Node can't use, so a small Go helper (`deploy/confidential/enclave-io`, standard library only, written for this repository) is the image's entry point.

The helper relays Unix sockets in `/run/keyhouse` to the parent's vsock ports, and the inbound port 8443 to the service:

| Parent vsock port | Carries |
| --- | --- |
| 8000 | KMS, through `vsock-proxy` |
| 8001 | The instance metadata service, for the role's credentials |
| 8002 | The settings file |
| 8003 | The log lines |

The helper alone opens `/dev/nsm`, the security module, and answers the service's attestation requests (the module's one `NSM_IOCTL_RAW` call, CBOR in and out). It runs the service as an unprivileged user.

AWS's own NSM library and `kmstool-enclave-cli` were the alternatives. Both would add a Rust or C toolchain and libraries to the measured image, where this helper is about 300 lines anyone can read.

### Settings from the parent

The settings (region, wrap key ARN, the client authority) come from the parent and aren't secret. All three are bound into every attestation, the authority as the SHA-256 of its certificate. A parent that names another key, or hands over an authority of its own, is seen by every verifier and refused by Mynt.

## Releases and the 48-hour wait

Each build of the service is what the hardware measures:

- for an enclave: PCR0 (the whole image file), PCR1 (kernel and boot ramdisk) and PCR2 (the application);
- for a container: its image digest.

### What CI builds

CI's `confidential-image` job builds the enclave image file (EIF) twice from scratch with `deploy/confidential/aws/build-eif.sh`: pinned base images, a pinned BuildKit, timestamps set to the commit's, and `nitro-cli` 1.5.3 in a pinned Amazon Linux container.

- It fails unless the PCRs match, and prints them with the commit.
- It also builds the Confidential Space image twice and compares digests.
- Nothing is pushed or deployed.

### Announcing a release

A Mynt admin announces a release with `announce_enclave_release { pcr0, pcr1, pcr2, release, reason }`, or `{ image_digest, … }` for a container. The announcement is:

- audited;
- told to every licence provider's firm: a notice to each member and `confidential.release_announced` on its webhooks;
- in effect only 48 hours later, the wait a mainnet program upgrade gets, so a partner can stop sending sealed statements first.

The first release ever is in effect at once: there is nothing before it. "First" means Mynt has no sign there was ever one before, not that the release table is empty. See [What enforces a release](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/confidential-computing.md#what-enforces-a-release).

| Tool | Who | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `announce_enclave_release` | Mynt admin | Announces a release |
| `withdraw_enclave_release` | Mynt admin | Takes one back |
| `list_enclave_releases` | Licence providers, liquidity providers, Mynt admins | Shows them all |

### What enforces a release

- Each row carries a MAC, so someone who can only write the database can't plant a build, bring a withdrawn one back by clearing its withdrawal, or move the moment one takes effect. A row that doesn't authenticate is never in effect.
- Mynt's server refuses to talk to a service whose attested measurements aren't in effect.
- The key policy is what finally decides which image can use the keys. Only the break-glass role changes it, and each change raises [the alarm on the key](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/confidential-computing.md#the-alarm-on-the-key).

Changing the key policy without announcing is possible for whoever holds the break-glass role. That is why partners verify the PCRs themselves and Mynt's server refuses unannounced ones.

### The key the release record is authenticated with

The release record decides whether the confidential service is trusted, so its MAC key has to be there before the service is. On a server set to a confidential service, the key is derived from the server's client key for that service (`CONFIDENTIAL_HOST_CLIENT_KEY`): a file the server already keeps, which someone who can only write the database doesn't have. On the local host it is derived from the vault, as before.

That is what lets a server start with `MYNT_VAULT_KEY` removed. At boot it authenticates the release rows with the client key, attests the service against them, and only then has the vault's keys released. If the client key can't be read, or the rows don't authenticate with it, no release is in effect and the server doesn't start: it never falls back to trusting the rows.

Rows written before this (authenticated with the vault-derived key) are authenticated again under the client key the first time the server opens the record with the vault key at hand, which every start during the migration does.

Replacing the client certificate changes that key. Start the server once with `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST_PREVIOUS_CLIENT_KEY` set to the old key's path: rows that authenticate under the old key are moved to the new one. Then remove the setting and destroy the old key. Without the old key the rows can't be carried over: announce the build again and wait the 48 hours.

### Withdrawals and an emptied table

A withdrawal is part of what a row's MAC covers. It is also recorded outside the row, in the audit log and in the running server's memory, and either record makes the release withdrawn whatever its row says.

An announcement is "the first", and in effect at once, only when all of these hold:

- the release table has no rows, authentic or not;
- the audit log has no record of a release being announced or withdrawn;
- the confidential host keeps nothing for Mynt (no wrapped root, no vault keys), which it can't before a release was in effect;
- this server hasn't had the vault released to it by a host.

So emptying the release table, or breaking every row's MAC, doesn't buy an immediate release.

What this can't prevent: someone who can delete from the release table, the audit log and the host's keys table together, on a server that doesn't hold a released vault, can still make it look like a first install. And someone who can rewrite both a release's row and the audit log's record of its withdrawal, and who kept a copy of the row from before it was withdrawn, can put it back once the server has restarted. Both need more than write access to one table, both leave the firms' notices of the original announcement and withdrawal standing, and neither gets an image past the attestation check or the key policy.

## Confidential computing settings

Settings are given by name only.

On Mynt's server:

| Setting | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST` | `local`, `aws-nitro` or `gcp-confidential-space`. Unset means `local` |
| `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST_URL` | `https://…:8443` of the parent instance's address |
| `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST_CLIENT_CERT`, `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST_CLIENT_KEY` | File paths, readable only by Mynt's user |
| `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST_CLIENT_CA` | A file path: the certificate of the authority that issued the client certificate (`ca.crt`). Public. Required for both remote hosts |
| `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST_KMS_KEY` | For `aws-nitro`: the wrap key's ARN. A name, not a secret. Required |
| `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST_WRAP_KEY` | For `gcp-confidential-space`: the name of the Cloud KMS key that wraps the service's root, as the VM's `KEYHOUSE_WRAP_KEY`. Required |
| `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST_SIGNING_KEYS` | For `gcp-confidential-space`: JSON naming each signing key's version, as the VM's `KEYHOUSE_SIGNING_KEYS`. Required |
| `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST_PREVIOUS_CLIENT_KEY` | A file path, set for one start after the client certificate is replaced: see [The key the release record is authenticated with](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/confidential-computing.md#the-key-the-release-record-is-authenticated-with) |

On the parent instance: `/etc/mynt-keyhouse/settings.json` (`region`, `kms_key`, `client_ca`), written by `deploy/confidential/aws/parent-setup.sh`. `client_ca` is exactly one certificate.

For Confidential Space, the VM's launcher overrides instead. They are the only names the image allows, and none is a secret: `KEYHOUSE_WIP_PROVIDER`, `KEYHOUSE_WRAP_KEY`, `KEYHOUSE_SIGNING_KEYS`, `KEYHOUSE_WRAPPED_ROOT`, `KEYHOUSE_CLIENT_CA`, `KEYHOUSE_PORT`.

## Operator steps for AWS Nitro Enclaves

One upload creates everything. No command here creates anything until the operator runs it, and none involves typing a secret into a chat.

1. **An AWS account.** Create an AWS account (or use one kept for Mynt alone), and pick one region for everything below, for example `us-east-1`.
2. **Mynt's client certificate.** On Mynt's server, run `deploy/confidential/make-client-cert.sh /etc/mynt/confidential` as Mynt's user. It writes Mynt's client certificate and key there (readable only by that user) and the authority's certificate (`ca.crt`, public). It prints two things to keep: one long line, the authority's certificate in base64, for step 5; and the authority's SHA-256, which partners need.
3. **The release.** Find the release's commit and PCRs: the `confidential-image` job's summary in CI shows the commit, `pcr0`, `pcr1` and `pcr2`. A Mynt admin announces them with `announce_enclave_release` (the first one is in effect at once).
4. **The break-glass role.** In the AWS console, open IAM and create a role that nobody holds day to day, to be assumed only for upgrades. It is the one principal allowed to change the wrap key's policy. Copy its ARN.
5. **The stack.** In the AWS console, open CloudFormation, choose **Create stack** → **With new resources**, and upload `deploy/confidential/aws/keyhouse.cloudformation.json`. Fill in:
   - `ReleaseCommit`: the commit;
   - `AllowedPcr0s`: the release's `pcr0`;
   - `MyntServerAddress`: Mynt's server's public address followed by `/32`;
   - `ClientAuthorityBase64`: the long line from step 2;
   - `KeyPolicyAdminRoleArn`: the ARN from step 4;
   - `AlarmEmail`: where the alarm on the key is sent;
   - `CreateAuditTrail`: leave `true` unless the account already has a CloudTrail trail recording management events in this region.

   Leave the rest as they are. Tick the box that lets it create a role, and create the stack. AWS emails `AlarmEmail` a confirmation link: click it, or the alarm stays silent.
6. **Mynt's settings.** When the stack shows `CREATE_COMPLETE`, its **Outputs** tab shows `ConfidentialHostUrl` and `WrapKeyArn`. On Mynt's server, set `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST=aws-nitro`, `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST_URL` (the first), `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST_KMS_KEY` (the second), `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST_CLIENT_CERT=/etc/mynt/confidential/client.crt`, `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST_CLIENT_KEY=/etc/mynt/confidential/client.key` and `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST_CLIENT_CA=/etc/mynt/confidential/ca.crt`, and restart Mynt. All of them are required: the server refuses to start with `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST=aws-nitro` and any one missing.
7. **What partners need.** Give each licence provider the wrap key's ARN (`WrapKeyArn`) and the authority's SHA-256 from step 2. They pass both to `verify-mynt-enclave`, which requires them.
8. **The root.** Run `mynt confidential status` (it shows the attested PCRs), then `mynt confidential init` once. The enclave makes its root, Mynt stores it wrapped, and it prints the wrapped form for you to keep a copy of.
9. **The vault.** Move the vault's keys to the service:
   1. Run `mynt confidential adopt`. The service adopts `MYNT_VAULT_KEY`.
   2. Restart Mynt. The vault's keys now come from the service at boot.
   3. Run `mynt confidential rewrap`. It is a dry run: counts per table and column, nothing changed.
   4. Run `mynt confidential rewrap --apply`.
   5. Run the dry run again to see zero left.
   6. Remove `MYNT_VAULT_KEY` from the server's environment file and restart. The server starts without it: the release record is authenticated with the client key, the service is attested, and the service releases the vault's keys.
   7. Destroy any copy of the old environment file kept elsewhere. Old database backups still hold values sealed with it.
10. **A new release.** Announce its PCRs and wait the 48 hours. Then assume the break-glass role (only it can change the key's policy) and, as that role, in CloudFormation choose the stack → **Update** → **Use current template**, set `ReleaseCommit` to the new commit and `AllowedPcr0s` to the old and new `pcr0` separated by a comma, and update. CloudFormation replaces the instance (same address), and Mynt hands the new enclave its root. Once it is running, update again with only the new `pcr0`. Each of the two updates raises the alarm on the key: these are the expected ones.

### What the stack makes

- one `c6a.xlarge` instance with enclaves enabled;
- the wrap key with the policy in [The key policy](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/confidential-computing.md#the-key-policy);
- the instance's role, with only `kms:Decrypt` and `kms:GenerateDataKey` on that key;
- a security group that admits only Mynt's server on port 8443;
- a fixed address;
- [the alarm on the key](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/confidential-computing.md#the-alarm-on-the-key): an SNS topic with the email subscription, an EventBridge rule and a CloudWatch alarm;
- unless `CreateAuditTrail` is `false`, a CloudTrail trail for management events in the region and a private bucket for its logs, kept 400 days.

It doesn't make the break-glass role: that one exists before the stack does, so the stack can't be used to hand it to anyone.

The instance builds the enclave from the commit on first boot (about ten minutes) and refuses to start it unless its PCR0 is the one you entered.

### Doing it by hand

To do it by hand instead, you need:

- an Amazon Linux 2023 instance of a type that supports enclaves, with 4 vCPUs: `c6a.xlarge`, `m6i.xlarge` and the like. Graviton types such as `c7g.large` support enclaves too, but this image is built for x86-64;
- **Nitro Enclave** enabled at launch, and IMDSv2 required;
- a role allowed only those two KMS calls on the wrap key;
- a symmetric KMS key with `key-policy.json` (fill in the account, the role's ARN, the break-glass role's ARN and the PCR0), set with the lockout safety check bypassed, since the account itself can't change the policy afterwards;
- an alarm of your own on `PutKeyPolicy` for that key, as the template's;
- port 8443 open to Mynt's server alone.

Then run `deploy/confidential/aws/parent-setup.sh` from a checkout of the release's commit. It installs `nitro-cli` 1.5.3 and the allocator settings (2 vCPUs and 3 GiB for the enclave), builds the EIF, and starts the enclave and its relays as systemd units.

### What it costs

These are approximate figures from AWS's public prices, not something Mynt measures:

| Item | Cost |
| --- | --- |
| The instance (`c6a.xlarge` in `us-east-1`) | About $0.153 an hour, about $112 a month on demand. A one-year savings plan takes roughly a third off |
| Its 30 GB disk | About $2.40 a month |
| Its public address | About $3.60 a month |
| The KMS key | $1 a month, plus $0.03 per 10,000 calls (a few a day) |
| The alarm, its rule and its emails | About $0.10 a month |
| The trail and its bucket | The first trail's management events are free; its logs cost cents a month to store |
| Nitro Enclaves | Nothing extra |

About $120 a month in all.

## Operator steps for Google Confidential Space

This is the alternative, with `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST=gcp-confidential-space`.

1. **A project.** In Google Cloud, create a project for the service and enable the Confidential Computing, Cloud KMS, IAM Credentials and Compute Engine APIs.
2. **Keys.** In Cloud KMS, create a key ring with a symmetric encrypt/decrypt key (the wrap key) and an asymmetric signing key with algorithm `EC_SIGN_ED25519` (the health attester).
3. **A workload identity pool.** Create a workload identity pool and an OIDC provider for it, with the values in [The OIDC provider](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/confidential-computing.md#the-oidc-provider).
4. **Key access for the attested image only.** Grant `roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter` on the wrap key and `roles/cloudkms.signerVerifier` on the signing key to the principal set in [Key access on Google Cloud](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/confidential-computing.md#key-access-on-google-cloud), and to nobody else.
5. **A service account.** Create a service account for the VM with only `roles/confidentialcomputing.workloadUser` and `roles/logging.logWriter`.
6. **Mynt's client certificate.** Make it with `deploy/confidential/make-client-cert.sh` (step 2 of the AWS steps) and put the authority's certificate (`ca.crt`, exactly one certificate) in the VM's `KEYHOUSE_CLIENT_CA`.
7. **The image.** Build the image from the release's commit (`docker buildx build --target confidential-space`, as CI's `confidential-image` job does), push it to Artifact Registry, and check the pushed digest equals the one CI printed. Then announce it (`announce_enclave_release { image_digest, … }`).
8. **The VM.** Create the VM from the `confidential-space` image family (never `confidential-space-debug`) with confidential computing on (N2D with SEV-SNP or C3 with TDX), shielded VM secure boot, and the service account above. Set the metadata `tee-image-reference` (the image by digest), `tee-restart-policy=Always`, `tee-container-log-redirect=true`, and the `tee-env-KEYHOUSE_*` settings, without `KEYHOUSE_WRAPPED_ROOT` yet. Only Mynt's server should reach its port (a firewall rule for that address only).
9. **Mynt's settings and the root.** On Mynt's server, set `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST=gcp-confidential-space`, `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST_URL`, the two certificate paths, `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST_CLIENT_CA` (the path to `ca.crt`), `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST_WRAP_KEY` (the same name as the VM's `KEYHOUSE_WRAP_KEY`) and `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST_SIGNING_KEYS` (the same JSON as the VM's `KEYHOUSE_SIGNING_KEYS`). All are required. Then run `mynt confidential init`. It prints the wrapped root. Set it as the VM's `tee-env-KEYHOUSE_WRAPPED_ROOT` and restart the VM. `mynt confidential status` then shows the attested digest.
10. **What partners need.** Give each licence provider the wrap key's name, each signing key's version and the authority's SHA-256. `verify-mynt-enclave` requires all three for a container.
11. **The vault.** Follow step 9 of the AWS steps (adopt, restart, rewrap).

### The OIDC provider

- **Issuer:** `https://confidentialcomputing.googleapis.com`
- **Allowed audience:** `https://sts.googleapis.com`
- **Attribute mapping**, two entries:
  - `google.subject = "gcpcs::" + assertion.submods.container.image_digest + "::" + assertion.submods.gce.project_number + "::" + assertion.submods.gce.instance_id`
  - `attribute.image_digest = assertion.submods.container.image_digest`
- **Attribute condition:** `assertion.swname == 'CONFIDENTIAL_SPACE' && 'STABLE' in assertion.submods.confidential_space.support_attributes && assertion.dbgstat == 'disabled-since-boot'`

Add `&& assertion.hwmodel == '<model>'` to the condition to pin the hardware.

### Key access on Google Cloud

The principal set that gets the two key roles is:

`principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/projects/<number>/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/<pool>/attribute.image_digest/<the release's digest>`

- No person, group or service account gets either role on those keys, and the project's owners are told not to add one.
- An owner could add one, so the project's IAM audit log is what shows it.
- Give a person `roles/cloudkms.viewer` and `roles/cloudkms.publicKeyViewer` if they need to see the keys exist.

## Not built yet

Phases 2 and 3 are not built. The same types carry over.

- **Build agents** will get an isolated VM per build behind `SandboxHost`, so a build's code and credentials are out of the operator's reach and Mynt can attest which image ran it.
- **Hosted apps** will get a confidential hosting tier: each app's enclave or VM attested the same way, its measurements announced through the same release record, and its attestation available to its users.

## Limits

- **It rests on the hardware and the cloud.** With Nitro Enclaves, AWS operates the hypervisor that isolates the enclave and the security module that signs its attestations, and runs KMS, which enforces the key policy. Trusting the service means trusting AWS for those.
- **The cloud account's administrators.** The AWS account's administrators can't read the enclave's memory or use the wrap key. They can't change the key policy as themselves, but they can take over the break-glass role that can, and then admit an image of their own to the wrap key. That raises the alarm and is recorded in CloudTrail; it isn't prevented. [What the key policy can't do](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/confidential-computing.md#what-the-key-policy-cant-do) has the detail. It is why partners check the PCRs, the wrap key and the client authority themselves and don't rely on the policy.
- **Confidential Space.** The same holds for Google, where the project's owners can grant themselves the key roles. AMD SEV-SNP and Intel TDX have had published attacks and firmware fixes, so the attestation's hardware and OS version matter.
- **The release record.** It is authenticated, but a record kept in one database can't prove its own history. [Withdrawals and an emptied table](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/confidential-computing.md#withdrawals-and-an-emptied-table) says what someone who can rewrite several tables at once could still do.
- **The server's client key.** Whoever can read `CONFIDENTIAL_HOST_CLIENT_KEY` on Mynt's server can call the service as Mynt's server does, and can authenticate release rows. It is a file readable only by Mynt's user, and it is all that stays on the server's disk.
- **The parent can deny service, never read.** The enclave's clock comes from its parent, and its logs go to the parent's journal (route, caller and outcome only). A parent can stop or restart the enclave, or refuse to relay.
- **Mynt's server still sees what it serves.** Entitled readers get figures through `get_product_health`, so a product's figures pass through Mynt's server on their way out. What it never sees is a partner's whole statement (every product's books) when sealed, or the vault's root.
- **Keys in the running process.** The vault's data key and derivation key are released to Mynt's running process. Someone with root on that server while it runs can read its memory. What changes is that they are no longer in a file, the environment or a backup.
- **The registered partner key.** The service trusts the partner key Mynt's server says is registered. A snapshot signed with another key fails, and the partner sees which key was used, so it can check.
- **Solana keys.** Solana keys Mynt holds (deploy authorities, the health publisher, the treasury attester) stay in the vault and sign in Mynt's process. Moving them to `signing-key` (signed inside the service) is not built.
- **In the clear.** The partner's daily-file upload and conformance stay in the clear.
- **Until the service is deployed.** Until the operator deploys the service, everything above runs on the local host, which protects nothing from whoever runs the server.

pages.title: Audits & compliance
pages.markdown:
## Compliance and the audit trail

Three read-only tools show what a workspace's apps rest on, and a fourth lists their obligations. All are for the workspace's members only. Nothing about other workspaces appears: only "available" says that someone else's product may be sold in a state.

### Coverage by state

`get_compliance_coverage` gives each of the 50 US states and DC a status, by Mynt's own product rules: the same ones `get_product_regime` and publishing apply.

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `unlocked` | A published product one of the workspace's apps uses may be sold there |
| `available` | Some other published product may be sold there |
| `unavailable` | None may |

A product may be sold in a state when:

- every regulated component of it is covered in the state by a licence that is verified and in force (its validity window), counting where the regulatory model says that licence counts, under an approved sponsorship where a licence provider provides the component; and
- its sales aren't paused. A covenant breach, or anything else that drifted it, pauses them everywhere.

An unlocked state lists the firms whose licences cover it, those licences, the products, and those firms' approved money rails there (kind, direction, provider, status; never limits). A workspace whose apps use no product sees only `available` and `unavailable`.

### Licences behind the products

`list_workspace_licences` lists the licences covering those products, as the coverage counts them: firm, type, regulator, number, the states they cover them in, status and expiry. Filter by `status`, `regulator` or `state`.

### The workspace audit trail

`list_workspace_audit` is the workspace's audit trail, newest first, paged with `next_cursor`. It returns up to 100 at a time. Filter by `action`, `user_id`, `app_id`, `from` and `to`, each of the last two a real calendar date or ISO time.

It holds what happened:

- to the workspace itself: members, invites, renames, offboarding;
- to its apps, and events that name one of them, like its keys and webhooks, deploys, hosting commands and releases;
- to their builds;
- in Mynt admins' decisions on its members' connections to its apps' repositories.

Events are chosen by what they are about, never by searching text.

- Details pass through Mynt's secret scrubber. Fields named like secrets, tokens, passwords, API or private keys, authorization or cookies are hidden.
- Whom an invite went to (its email and id) is shown to owners and admins only.
- The cursor keeps the database's full timestamp precision, so events in the same instant all come back.

### Audit classes

Each event is `{ id, at, class, kind, actor, app_id?, target, summary, severity?, status?, details }`. `action` is kept, the same as `kind`.

`class` comes from one table, `core/src/audit-classes.ts`, keyed by action. An action in no list is `workspace`. `core/test/audit-classes.test.js` reads every audit action in the source and fails on one that isn't in the table.

| Class | Covers |
| --- | --- |
| `security` | Application security: Mynt's independent build audits, repository access and its checks, the mainnet program gate and its vulnerability flags, secrets revealed or rotated (including out of a leaver's reach), VM logins and container exec, the hosting kill switch, and account recovery |
| `obligations` | Financial licence obligations: licences and the firm's governance, risk and compliance (GRC) records against them, firm checks, sponsorships, covenants and their breaches, product composition and drift, target states, production sign-offs (tied to licences and money rails), governance review, and the regulatory model |
| `financial` | Financial activity: money movements and their refusals, live hand-offs, liquidity commitments, withdrawals and pool state, money rails and ramps, partner ledgers, program calls and take rates |
| `workspace` | Running the workspace: members, roles and invites, apps, builds, promotions, hosting, keys and webhooks, and settings |

`class` filters by it. Without `class` you get every event.

Three kinds of row come from Mynt's own records, not the audit log:

- `build_audit` (security): each build of the workspace's apps that Mynt's independent audit ran on, at the time the build finished. `severity` is its worst finding (`critical`, `high`, `medium`, `low` or `none`) and `status` the build's.
- `money_movement` and `handoff` (financial): live ones only, never sandbox, with what moved and how it ended (`status`). Never a customer or rail reference.

`severity` is also set where the action itself says it:

- `high` for a covenant breach, a paused product, a program review flag or withdrawn repository access;
- `medium` for a pool flag or a refused, stale or differing money movement.

Otherwise it is absent.

In Mynt Studio, the Audits page shows these classes as the tabs App security, Licence obligations, Financial activity and Workspace activity, with Agreement audits beside them (see [Audits](https://github.com/never2average/mynt/blob/main/docs/reference/studio.md#audits)).

### Licence obligations

`get_workspace_obligations({ workspace_id })` lists the obligations in the regulator's own register for each licence covering a product the workspace's apps use, as `list_workspace_licences` counts them. The register is `grc.registers.obligations` of the licence type, as the regulatory model defines it.

Each is `{ licence_id, licence_type, partner: { entity_id, name }, regulator, obligation_id, title, products: [{ id, name }], status, evidence?, reason? }`.

`status` comes only from what the licence holder recorded in Mynt:

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `overdue` | A filing the register ties to the obligation (`obligation_ref`) was recorded overdue |
| `met` | Its obligation record says compliant |
| `at_risk` | Its obligation record says partially or non-compliant |
| `unknown`, with a `reason` | Nothing recorded, not assessed, or marked not applicable (the firm's say-so, which Mynt can't confirm) |

`evidence` says what the record says and when, and how many evidence items it has, never their text. Mynt records no due dates, so `due_at` isn't given.

## Oversight audits

A program agreement also says which **oversight audits** its licence provider runs on the app: an annual compliance review, a quarterly complaints review, a review of the marketing material on each change.

An agreement has many audit requirements. Each requirement has many audits over time, one open at a time.

The tools are in `core/src/agreement-audits.ts`. The tables (`agreement_audit_requirements`, `agreement_audits`) are in `core/src/agreement-audits-schema.ts`.

These audits are the agreement's own, not the regulator's. The regulatory obligations under `get_workspace_obligations` keep their register's schema and aren't changed by them.

### Audit requirements

A requirement is managed by a licence provider: a member of the agreement's counterparty firm with licence-provider standing.

`add_agreement_audit_requirement({ agreement_id, name, kind, cadence, first_due?, description?, evidence_required? })` adds one to a `program` agreement that is proposed, accepted or signed. So requirements can come with the licence provider's terms before it signs.

| Field | Values |
| --- | --- |
| `kind` | `compliance_review`, `complaints_review`, `marketing_review`, `security_review`, `financial_review`, `other` |
| `cadence` | `once`, `monthly`, `quarterly`, `annual`, `on_change` |
| `first_due` | YYYY-MM-DD. Required except for `on_change`, which has none |

At most 50 live requirements per agreement.

`retire_agreement_audit_requirement({ requirement_id, reason })` stops one. Its open audit is waived with that reason, and closed ones stay.

### Scheduling

Audits run only under a signed agreement. A timer (every minute, `sweepAgreementAudits`), and each add and close, opens a requirement's next audit (`scheduled`) when it has none open.

| Cadence | Next audit |
| --- | --- |
| `once` | One audit, due on `first_due` |
| `monthly`, `quarterly`, `annual` | Due on `first_due`, then a month, three months or a year after the previous one's due date (the day clamped to the month's end). It opens 14, 30 or 60 days before it is due |
| `on_change` | Opens when the app's builds give it new verified source: a succeeded build whose source SHA-256 differs from the one the last audit was opened for. Due 30 days later. The licence provider can also open one by hand |

Mynt can't tell which files customers see, so every new verified source counts as a change.

A due date runs to the end of its day, UTC.

### An audit's life

An audit is `scheduled`, `in_progress`, `submitted`, then `passed`, `failed` or `waived`.

| Tool | Who | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `open_agreement_audit({ audit_id })` | Licence provider | Opens a scheduled audit. It is in progress and the caller is its reviewer |
| `open_agreement_audit({ requirement_id, due? })` | Licence provider | Opens one by hand, due on `due` or 30 days from now. Refused while that requirement has one open |
| `submit_agreement_audit_evidence({ audit_id, evidence: [{ name, url, sha256 }], note? })` | The app's workspace owners and admins | Adds evidence. The audit becomes `submitted` |
| `record_agreement_audit_finding({ audit_id, severity, title, detail? })` | Licence provider | Adds an open finding and sends a scheduled or submitted audit back to `in_progress`. `severity` is `low`, `medium`, `high` or `critical` |
| `respond_to_agreement_audit_finding({ audit_id, finding_id, response })` | Owners and admins | Answers a finding |
| `resolve_agreement_audit_finding({ audit_id, finding_id, note? })` | Licence provider | Resolves a finding |
| `close_agreement_audit({ audit_id, outcome, note? })` | Licence provider | Closes the audit |

Evidence is https links with their SHA-256. Mynt keeps links and hashes, not files. At most 20 at a time and 50 per audit.

Closing: `passed` only once the audit is `submitted` and every finding is resolved; `failed` or `waived` at any point, with a note saying why. The requirement's next audit then opens when its time comes.

### Reading audits

Only the agreement's two parties read its audits: any member of the app's workspace, and the counterparty firm's licence providers.

`list_agreement_audits({ workspace_id?, app_id?, agreement_id?, status?, overdue?, side? })` returns `{ requirements, audits, counts: { audits, open, overdue } }`:

- each requirement with its counterparty, how many audits it has had, its next due date and whether it is overdue;
- each audit with its requirement, agreement, app and counterparty, `overdue`, `findings_open`, `your_side` and `actions`.

`actions` is what the caller may do next: `open`, `record_finding`, `resolve_finding`, `pass`, `fail`, `waive`, `submit_evidence`, `respond_to_finding`.

`get_agreement_audit({ audit_id })` adds the people named and its `history`: every audit-log entry for it, who made it and when. The schedule's own entries have no actor.

### Overdue audits

Overdue means past its due date and not closed. A submitted audit waiting for review still counts.

An overdue audit flags the app:

- `get_workspace_attention` lists it as `agreement_audit_overdue`;
- `ops_status` counts overdue audits and the apps they are on (`agreement_audits`);
- the lists mark it.

### Audit trail and events for oversight audits

Every change is audited with the app's id, in the obligations class: `add_agreement_audit_requirement`, `retire_agreement_audit_requirement`, `agreement_audit_scheduled`, `open_agreement_audit`, `submit_agreement_audit_evidence`, `record_agreement_audit_finding`, `respond_to_agreement_audit_finding`, `resolve_agreement_audit_finding`, `pass_agreement_audit`, `fail_agreement_audit`, `waive_agreement_audit`.

Both parties' firms are told on their webhooks and notices:

| Event | When |
| --- | --- |
| `agreement_audit.opened` | Opened by the schedule or the licence provider |
| `agreement_audit.submitted` | Evidence or an answer from the app's side |
| `agreement_audit.closed` | Closed, with its outcome |

## Legal entities

Every firm on Mynt is a legal entity. Its record feeds the regime check on every product that rests on it.

### Facts

A legal entity is recorded as typed facts, never prose:

| Fact | How it is recorded |
| --- | --- |
| Legal form | From a fixed list |
| Incorporation | Lowercase ISO 3166 codes such as `in` or `in-mh` |
| Identifiers | `{ scheme, value }` pairs, for example `in_cin`, `lei` or `us_ein` |
| Status | Set by Mynt admins from the company registry |
| Licences held | Verified by Mynt admins |

### Parties

Each entity keeps a party roster (`add_party`, `end_party`):

- **Internal** parties are people, such as the compliance officer.
- **External** parties are other legal entities, such as the statutory auditor or a lending partner.

A party fills the mandatory stakeholders that the licence type of a held licence requires (`grc.mandatory_stakeholders` in the regulatory model). It may also be a counterparty, with a relationship code.

Parties aren't edited. To change one, end it and add a new one.

`get_my_entity` lists the roster, naming the firm behind each external party (`legal_entity_name`), and reconciles each held licence against it. It reports:

- which mandated stakeholders are filled, and by whom;
- which are missing;
- which parties fail the stakeholder's qualification criteria;
- which parties have no stated facts for those criteria.

### GRC folders
